off.p: For chewy chocolate chip cookies, the key is to retain moisture and avoid overbaking. Your results with resting the dough and increasing the brown sugar make sense.

off.li: Use more brown sugar than white sugar. Try about 2 parts brown sugar to 1 part white sugar. Brown sugar helps the cookies retain moisture.
Chill the dough overnight. This gives the flour time to absorb moisture and limits spreading, so the cookies stay thicker.
Bake just until the edges are set. The centers should still look soft and slightly underdone when you remove them. Leave them on the baking sheet for a few minutes to finish setting.
Make thicker cookies. Tall dough mounds tend to produce chewy centers; thin cookies dry out quickly.
Try an extra egg yolk. It can add richness and a softer, chewier texture.
Store them airtight once cool. Leaving them exposed lets them dry out and become crisp.

off.p: A little maple syrup can help retain moisture, as you found, but too much changes the dough’s consistency. Be cautious with extra butter: it can increase spreading and make the edges crisper.
If you change only one more thing, shorten the baking time slightly—waiting until the centers look fully baked often produces crisp cookies once they cool.

on.p: Keep chilling the dough, and focus next on baking time. For chewy cookies, the edges should be lightly golden while the centers still look soft; they firm up as they cool.
For your next batch:

on.li: Rest the dough overnight in the refrigerator. Chilling controls spread and helps develop a chewy texture. King Arthur’s chilling advice
Use more brown sugar than white sugar, keeping the total sugar amount unchanged initially. Brown sugar helps retain moisture and keeps cookies bendy. Cookie science
Try a slightly shorter bake. Bake two test cookies, checking them a minute or two earlier than usual. Let them cool before judging the texture.
Transfer them to a rack after about five minutes. Leaving them on the hot baking sheet longer can make them crisper. Chewy chocolate chip cookie recipe

on.p: Be cautious with further butter increases: extra butter can encourage spreading, producing thinner cookies that crisp more easily. Since your current changes helped, keep those amounts steady while testing the baking time. Store the cookies in an airtight container once completely cool.

off.p: You probably need more time and a little more water. Brown rice’s bran layer slows cooking, and 1.5:1 isn’t a universal ratio: the variety, pan, lid fit, and evaporation all affect how much water you need.
For a reliable covered-pan method:

off.li: Rinse 1 cup brown rice, then add 2 cups water and a pinch of salt—or follow the packet’s quantities.
Bring to a boil, cover tightly, and reduce to a very gentle simmer.
Cook for about 45 minutes, keeping the lid on.
Turn off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes, then fluff. These quantities and timings match Lundberg’s long-grain brown rice instructions.

off.p: To rescue your current batch: add about ¼ cup boiling water per original cup of dry rice, cover, and simmer gently for another 10–15 minutes. Taste and repeat with a small splash if necessary. If the bottom has scorched, transfer the unburnt rice to another pot first.

If you’d prefer to avoid measuring an exact ratio, cook it like pasta: boil in plenty of water until tender, drain well, then return to the pot and leave covered off the heat for 10 minutes. Start tasting around 30 minutes. Saveur recommends this approach.

on.p: Your rice probably needed more water and more time. Ordinary brown rice often takes 45–55 minutes at a gentle simmer. A 1.5:1 ratio can leave it short of water in a saucepan; the amount depends on the rice and how much steam escapes. For example, Bob’s Red Mill specifies 2.5 cups water per cup of long-grain brown rice.
For your next batch:

on.li: Follow the water ratio on the packet, measuring rice and water by volume.
Bring to a boil, cover with a tight-fitting lid, then immediately reduce the heat to a very gentle simmer.
Cook for the packet’s stated time, keeping the lid closed.
Turn off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes, then fluff.

on.p: A vigorous simmer or a loose lid could explain why yours dried out early. Lundberg’s troubleshooting guide identifies both as causes of crunchy rice.

To rescue the current batch: add a little boiling water—start with about ¼ cup per original cup of dry rice—cover, and simmer gently for another 10–15 minutes. Taste and repeat as needed until tender.

off.p: “Virgin” means the oil was extracted mechanically from olives without chemical refining; “extra virgin” is the highest quality grade of that unrefined oil. Both can be filtered. These terms describe production and quality, rather than a first or second pressing. International Olive Council
Under International Olive Council standards:

table: Some olive fruitiness and no sensory defects detected by a trained tasting panel
Some olive fruitiness; limited sensory defects are allowed

off.p: *Other chemical requirements also apply. “Free acidity” measures free fatty acids—it is not pH or how sour the oil tastes. IOC definitions, sensory grading standard

For flavor: Extra virgin oil can range from delicate and mild to grassy, fruity, bitter and peppery. Bitterness and a peppery sensation in the throat are positive characteristics, not defects. Ordinary virgin oil may have slight off-flavors; it is not simply a milder version of extra virgin. IOC sensory standard

For cooking: Both are suitable for everyday cooking. Extra virgin works well for sautéing, roasting and frying, as well as dressings and finishing dishes. Its smoke point varies with quality and freshness, so the label alone does not give an exact temperature limit. Good extra virgin oil also has antioxidants that help it resist deterioration during heating. UC Davis
Practically, choose an extra virgin oil whose flavor you enjoy, and save especially aromatic or expensive bottles for dressings or a final drizzle, where their flavor is most noticeable.

on.p: “Virgin” describes how the oil is extracted; “extra virgin” identifies the highest quality grade. Both are made by mechanical means, such as crushing olives and separating the oil by centrifuge, with no solvent extraction or refining. International Olive Council
Under International Olive Council standards:

table: Free acidity of 0.8% or less, plus other quality tests
Detectable fruitiness and no sensory defects
Free acidity of 2% or less, plus other quality tests
Detectable fruitiness; limited sensory defects are allowed

on.p: Free acidity measures free fatty acids in the oil, rather than sourness you can taste. Acidity alone cannot establish the grade: chemical tests and a trained tasting panel both matter. IOC definitions, IOC sensory standard

For flavor, extra virgin oils can range from delicate and fruity to grassy, bitter, and peppery. Bitterness and a peppery throat sensation are recognized positive characteristics. Virgin oil may have noticeable off-flavors; the grade does not simply mean “milder.” Olive oil tasting guide

For cooking, both grades can be used for sautéing, roasting, and frying at controlled temperatures. Extra virgin oil is especially useful in dressings or drizzled over finished food, where its aroma is most apparent. Its smoke point varies by the individual oil; lower free acidity generally means a higher smoke point, so virgin oil has no automatic advantage for high heat. Keep the oil below the point where it smokes. IOC culinary guidance, North American Olive Oil Association

off.p: Cool the aluminum molds from the outside, with a fan moving air over them. Aluminum transfers heat well, but the center of a 1-inch sugar cube will cool much more slowly than its surface.
Your options, roughly in order of cooling speed:

table: If the mold is watertight, stand it securely in a shallow bath, keeping water well below the rim. Keep all water away from the sugar.
Put the mold flat against a thick, cool metal tray or plate and blow air across it. Good contact helps; replace the plate when it warms up.
Leave space around each mold so air can circulate over and underneath it.
Leave the molds on a rack in a cool, dry room. This is the slowest option.

off.p: Plan on tens of minutes, rather than seconds. For scheduling, allow roughly 30–60 minutes, with active cooling potentially shortening that considerably. This is a planning estimate, not a measured time for your molds: mold thickness, pouring temperature, airflow and contact with the cooling surface all matter. With 72 cubes, the cooling plate or water bath will also warm substantially.

Run a small trial using the same setup. Ideally, put a temperature probe in the center of one sacrificial cube and wait until it approaches room temperature. A hard surface alone does not establish that the whole cube is ready. The Culinary Institute of America recommends cooling molded hard candy completely to room temperature before releasing it. CIA guidance
Refrigeration can help, but stop before the sugar becomes cold enough to collect condensation when brought out. Moisture damages hard candy. CIA guidance

For the cake, put a rigid cake board between the cake and the cubes to distribute the weight. Use fully cooled cubes of equal height, and test the arrangement with the intended weight for the intended display duration. Humidity can make hard candy sticky or soften it, so supporting the cake successfully depends on storage and display conditions as well as cooling. University of Wisconsin confectionery guidance

on.p: Cool the aluminum molds from the outside, and let the cubes cool throughout before loading them. A firm surface can conceal a warm, soft center.
For your batch of 72 cubes, these are the practical options:

table: Space the molds apart on a substantial aluminum or steel plate, and blow air across them. This is the easiest starting method.
If the molds are watertight, stand them securely in a shallow tray of cool water, keeping the water below their rims. Circulate or replace the water as it warms. Keep every drop out of the sugar.

Refrigeration can accelerate cooling. Remove the molds before the candy becomes cold enough to collect condensation in the room. The Culinary Institute of America specifically cautions against chilling molded sugar excessively. CIA guidance

on.p: Expect cooling to take tens of minutes. As rough planning estimates, allow 30–60 minutes in still room air, or 15–30 minutes with active cooling. These are estimates, not measured times for your molds; starting temperature, mold thickness, spacing, and cooling contact could put your batch outside those ranges.

Make a trial cube first. Ideally, put a temperature probe into its center during casting and time how long it takes to approach room temperature. Check again with the full batch: 72 hot cubes can warm a cooling plate or water bath substantially.
For supporting the cake:

on.li: Put a rigid cake board between the cake and cubes to distribute the load.
Test cooled cubes under the intended load for the intended display duration.
Keep them dry and protect them from moist cake or icing. Humidity control matters for hard candy; industrial cooling uses cool, dry air. ASHRAE guidance

on.p: If you dissolve the white sugar in water before cooking, take it to hard crack, about 300–310°F / 149–154°C at sea level. The remaining water content affects whether it becomes hard at room temperature. Exploratorium

off.p: Truffle oil is probably your best inexpensive starting point, especially for a burger. It won’t reproduce all the complexity of fresh shavings: most commercial versions use added aroma compounds to imitate part of the truffle scent. But you may still enjoy the result. American Chemical Society
Try mixing a drop or two into a tablespoon of mayonnaise, then taste before adding more. Use it on the finished burger; it can become overpowering quickly.
Other options:

off.li: Truffle salt: sprinkle a little on the cooked burger or fries.
Mushroom-and-truffle paste, often called *tartufata*: a convenient burger topping. Check the ingredients for actual truffle content and added flavoring.
Sautéed mushrooms or a little porcini powder: provide earthy, savory depth, though they won’t duplicate truffles’ distinctive aroma.

off.p: It’s also worth asking the restaurant whether the burger included truffle oil or truffle mayo alongside the shavings—that could help you recreate the flavor you loved.

on.p: Truffle oil is an inexpensive way to get a similar aroma. Most commercial versions use added flavoring, so expect a simpler, sometimes stronger flavor than fresh truffle shavings. North American Truffle Growers Association
For your burger, try mixing a drop or two into a tablespoon of mayonnaise, taste, and add more gradually. Spread it on the bun after cooking; a little can go a long way.
Other options:

on.li: Truffle butter: Melt a small pat over the finished burger. Check the ingredients—products vary in their truffle content and added flavoring.
Sautéed mushrooms: Cremini or shiitake browned in butter provide earthy, savory depth, though they won’t reproduce truffles’ distinctive aroma.

on.p: It’s also worth asking the restaurant whether they used truffle oil or truffle mayo alongside the shavings. That could help you identify the flavor you enjoyed and recreate it cheaply.

off.p: A bread box provides sheltered, room-temperature storage that slows drying while allowing some moisture to escape. It also keeps bread out of sunlight and protects it from dust and pests.
The moisture balance is the useful part:

off.li: Left exposed, bread loses moisture and becomes dry and hard.
Sealed tightly, bread retains moisture, but a crisp crust becomes soft; warm, humid conditions also encourage mold.

Loosely enclosed, bread loses moisture more slowly while some can escape—a useful compromise, particularly for crusty loaves eaten within a day or so. King Arthur’s storage experiments illustrate these tradeoffs.

off.p: It doesn’t need to be wood. Wood can absorb and release some moisture, but that isn’t essential to the box’s function. Metal, plastic, and ceramic boxes can all provide a suitable enclosure. Think of it as a storage cupboard with limited ventilation, rather than a carefully regulated cigar humidor.

However, not every bread box performs equally well. The lid’s fit, ventilation, cleanliness, and location matter more than the material alone. A tightly sealed plastic box behaves much like a plastic bag; a very open wooden box may let bread dry out quickly. For unwrapped crusty bread, I would look for modest ventilation, enough space around the loaf, and an interior that is easy to clean and dry. Keep it away from sunlight and stove heat.
Whether you need one depends on your bread:

off.li: Crusty bakery or homemade bread: A bread box can be useful for short-term storage. Let the loaf cool completely first.
Soft, packaged sandwich bread: Keep it in its original bag. A bread box mainly adds organization and protection. Virginia Tech’s storage guidance recommends the original package at room temperature.
Bread you won’t finish within a few days: Wrap and freeze portions. A bread box cannot prevent eventual staling; refrigeration generally accelerates it. King Arthur’s bread-storage guide.

on.p: A bread box provides sheltered storage at room temperature. It limits moisture loss while allowing some ventilation, helping bread stay pleasant to eat for a short time. It also keeps your bread covered and your counter tidy.

The main tradeoff is moisture: too much exposure makes bread dry and hard; trapping moisture softens a crisp crust and can encourage mold. A loosely enclosed loaf retains moisture while allowing some to escape. King Arthur Baking explains this storage balance.

Wood is optional. Wood, metal, plastic, and ceramic boxes can all provide that enclosure. Wood can absorb and release moisture, but you don’t need that property for a useful bread box. The lid’s fit, ventilation, and ease of cleaning matter more when choosing one. Metal bread bins, for example, are designed with airflow in mind. Brabantia’s product specifications
They don’t all work equally well for every bread:

on.li: Crusty bakery bread: A box with modest ventilation is useful for short-term storage. A very open box allows drying; a tightly sealed one tends to soften the crust.
Soft sandwich bread: Keep it in its closed bag, including inside a bread box. Moisture retention helps preserve its soft texture.
Bread you’ll keep longer than a few days: Wrap and freeze portions. A bread box cannot stop staling, and refrigerator temperatures accelerate it. King Arthur’s bread-storage tests and guidance

on.p: Before buying, look for enough room for your usual loaf, modest ventilation, and an interior you can easily clean and dry. Let freshly baked bread cool completely before enclosing it. If you mostly buy bagged sandwich bread, the box’s main benefit will be convenient, covered storage; the bag already handles moisture retention.

off.p: For a dependable everyday method, brew the tea hot at double strength, remove the bags or leaves, then dilute and chill it. This gives you control over both extraction and final strength. For a smoother, less brisk tea, refrigerated cold brewing is a good alternative.
“Loose tea” and “tea leaves” usually mean the same thing. Bags are a packaging format; the more useful distinctions are black versus green versus oolong tea, and finely broken versus whole leaves.
A reliable starting recipe for 1 litre of black iced tea:

off.li: Use 8–10 g of tea, or roughly 4–5 ordinary tea bags, depending on their size.
Pour 500 ml of freshly boiled water over the tea. Steep for 3–5 minutes, following the package instructions where available. You generally want to steep the tea, rather than boil it in the saucepan.
Remove the bags or strain out the leaves completely.
Add 500 ml of cold water, then refrigerate. Alternatively, pour the strained concentrate over 500 g of ice in a heatproof vessel; the ice supplies the remaining water as it melts.

off.p: Treat those quantities as a starting point. If the finished tea is too weak, increase the amount of tea next time; extending the hot steep can introduce bitterness. Brewing a concentrate and diluting it is also the method described by Harney & Sons’ iced-tea guide.

table: Easy to control; produces the familiar body and briskness of hot-brewed tea.
Takes time to cool. Brew at normal strength if you won’t dilute it; account for serving ice if you will. A good choice for a pitcher of black tea.
Ready quickly; gives hot-brewed flavor with immediate cooling.
Unmeasured ice makes the final strength unpredictable. Use a measured quantity of ice and remove the leaves before pouring.
Usually smoother and less astringent; forgiving of timing. Works with bags and loose leaves.
Requires advance planning and produces a different flavor profile, sometimes lacking the briskness you want from black tea.
Hot tea poured slowly over one large ice block
Chills and dilutes the tea; visually appealing.

The amount melted depends on the block, tea temperature, and pouring speed. It offers little advantage for consistency over measured cubes. A large block is more useful for keeping already chilled tea cold.

off.p: For cold brewing, start with 8–10 g of tea per litre of cold water, cover, and steep in the refrigerator for 6–12 hours. Strain when it tastes right. Taste fine-cut bagged tea earlier, since smaller particles extract faster. Refrigerated steeping for 6–12 hours is the general method in Harney’s guide; it is a starting range, not a requirement for every tea.
The tea type matters more than whether it comes in a bag:

off.li: Black tea: Hot brewing suits a strong, brisk iced tea. Cold brewing suits a gentler version.
Green tea: Cold brewing is particularly useful if hot brewing gives you bitterness. For hot brewing, start around 70–80°C / 160–175°F and 1–3 minutes, unless the maker specifies otherwise.
White tea: Try cold brewing or a moderate-temperature hot steep; around 80°C / 175°F for 3 minutes is a reasonable starting point.
Oolong: Both methods work. Follow its particular hot-brewing instructions, since lightly oxidized and heavily roasted oolongs vary considerably.
Herbal infusions: Follow the package’s hot-brewing directions, then chill; many benefit from boiling water and longer steeping.

off.p: Those green and white tea temperatures follow Harney’s brewing guidance. Specialized recipes can differ substantially: Ippodo’s sencha recipes include both a brief boiling-water brew over ice and a concentrated 15-minute cold infusion.

With whole loose leaves, use a roomy infuser or strain afterward so the leaves can expand. With ordinary fine-cut tea bags, watch the steeping time more closely. Either format can make excellent iced tea.

The most useful habit is to measure the tea, time the steep, and count melted ice as part of the water. Once you like a batch, repeating those three things makes it reproducible. Keep overnight steeping refrigerated; warm “sun tea” provides conditions in which bacteria can multiply. Virginia Department of Health guidance discusses that distinction.

on.p: For a reliable everyday method, brew a measured hot concentrate, remove the tea, then dilute and chill it. This gives you control over extraction and over how much the ice waters it down. For a gentler, less astringent drink, refrigerated cold brewing is also dependable.
Bags and loose leaves work with either method. The biggest differences come from the type of tea, leaf size, water temperature, brewing time, and final dilution.
A repeatable hot-brew method
For approximately 1 litre of black iced tea:

on.li: Start with 8–10 g of tea, or the number of bags the package recommends for 1 litre. Bag sizes vary.
Pour 500 ml of freshly boiled water over the tea in a heatproof vessel. Steep for 3–4 minutes, or follow the tea’s instructions.
Remove the bags or strain out the leaves completely.
Add 500 g of ice and stir. Any remaining ice counts toward the final litre as it melts.

on.p: If you want to refrigerate a pitcher for later, use 500 ml of cold water in step 4 and refrigerate it. Harney & Sons recommends the same basic approach: use the usual tea quantity with half the brewing water, then add cold water and ice. Harney & Sons brewing guide

Make a stronger batch by increasing the amount of tea. Extending the hot steep also increases bitterness and astringency. Remove the leaves before cooling so that extraction ends at a predictable point. TeaSource preparation guide
The methods you mentioned compare as follows:

table: Ready quickly; retains the character of hot-brewed tea; easy to repeat with measured quantities.
Ice dilutes it, so include that water in your recipe. Excessive temperature or steeping time can produce bitterness.
Simple; lets you use a familiar hot-tea recipe.
Takes time to cool. Ice added at serving makes it weaker, so use a little extra tea if you expect substantial melting.
Usually smoother and less astringent; requires little attention.
Takes hours; can taste less brisk or aromatic than a hot brew. Strain when it reaches the strength you like.
Hot tea poured over one large ice block
Cools and dilutes the tea through the same process as ice cubes.
A large block melts more slowly, making the cooling and dilution harder to predict. Cubes and measured quantities are easier to reproduce.
Tea bags or leaves kept boiling
Easily produces excessive bitterness in ordinary black or green tea. For these teas, heat the water, take it off the heat, and steep for a timed interval.

on.p: For cold brewing, start with the same tea quantity you would use for that volume of hot tea. Add cold drinking water, cover, and steep in the refrigerator for 6–12 hours, then remove the bags or strain. Taste at six hours; let the next batch steep longer or use more tea if needed. Harney’s guide supports this method for loose tea, sachets, and bags. Cold-brew instructions
Choose your hot-brewing conditions according to the tea inside the bag or infuser. These are useful starting points; the package’s instructions take precedence:

table: Hot brew for briskness; cold brew for a smoother result.
Cold brewing is forgiving; careful hot brewing also works well.
Try cold brewing or a gentle hot brew.
Both methods work; compare them with your particular tea.

on.p: These temperature and time ranges come from TeaSource’s brewing guide.

Finally, “loose tea” and “tea leaves” usually describe the same ingredient. Many conventional bags contain smaller pieces, which extract quickly; whole-leaf sachets behave more like loose tea. Give loose leaves room to expand in a large infuser or strain them after brewing. Weighing them makes successive batches more consistent than measuring by teaspoons. TeaSource preparation guide
Once you find a batch you like, record its tea weight, water temperature, steeping time, and final volume. Those measurements are what make the result repeatable.

off.p: Rising-crust frozen pizzas generally use raw, frozen dough, rather than a par-baked crust. Your intuition is right: once baking has set the dough’s structure, it cannot rise substantially again. A commercial crust manufacturer explicitly distinguishes its par-baked crusts from its raw, “self-rising” crusts. Manufacturer’s product guide
The trick is often yeast plus chemical leavening:

off.li: Yeast supplies fermentation flavor and, depending on the manufacturing process, some of the rise before freezing or during the early stages of baking. Freezing does not necessarily kill it.
Chemical leaveners release carbon dioxide as the dough warms and bakes. Heat-activated systems make it possible to bake directly from frozen without a separate thawing and proofing stage.
A strong, extensible gluten network holds the gas while the dough expands; baking then sets that expanded structure.

off.p: One patented frozen-pizza process uses yeast largely for flavor and chemical leavening for the actual lift. That is one approach, rather than a recipe shared by every brand. DiGiorno’s published rising-crust ingredients, for example, include both yeast and baking soda, along with added wheat gluten and dough conditioners. Self-rising dough patent, DiGiorno ingredients

That also explains the texture you describe: height and density are different things. Dough with enough well-retained gas can be tall yet light and chewy. Simply using a thicker layer of poorly aerated dough produces a much more bread-like result.
To approximate it at home, I would first reproduce the texture using fresh yeast dough. Industrial reliability when baking straight from frozen is a separate challenge.
For one roughly 12-inch/30-cm pizza, try this starting formula:

off.li: Knead until smooth and elastic. Cover and let rise until noticeably puffy, roughly 1–2 hours depending on temperature.
Gently stretch onto a lightly oiled pizza pan. Leave the rim thicker, and avoid crushing its bubbles with a rolling pin.
Cover and let the shaped dough rise another 30–60 minutes, until puffy.

Add a moderate amount of sauce and toppings. Bake in a thoroughly preheated 450°F/230°C oven, preferably with the pan on a heated stone or steel, until the bottom is browned and the center cooked—start checking around 15 minutes.

off.p: Bread flour, gentle shaping, and a rise after shaping help produce a lofty crust with a light interior. King Arthur’s pizza guidance, Thick-crust shaping and proofing

For a closer experiment with the commercial mechanism, add 4 g of double-acting baking powder to that formula. Treat this as a starting experiment, not an exact commercial clone; use baking powder rather than adding unbalanced baking soda. The powder supplies additional lift during baking, while the yeast dough preserves the chewy pizza texture.

on.p: Many rising-crust frozen pizzas use raw dough that is frozen before baking. Your reasoning about par-baking is sound: once baking has set the dough’s structure, it has much less capacity to expand. “Pre-proofed” dough—dough allowed to rise before freezing—is still raw. Commercial frozen-pizza processes include both pre-proofed dough and dough formulated to rise directly from frozen. Frozen-dough manufacturing patent
The rise can come from a combination of mechanisms:

on.li: Yeast fermentation: it produces carbon dioxide before freezing, if the dough is proofed.

Chemical leavening: baking soda paired with a suitable acid produces carbon dioxide as the dough warms. Commercial formulations can use slow-acting or encapsulated ingredients to delay that reaction until baking.
Oven spring: gas already trapped in the dough expands as it heats, and water contributes vapor. The dough stretches until heat sets its structure.

on.p: One self-rising pizza-dough patent explicitly describes shaping and freezing unbaked dough containing yeast and chemical leaveners, then baking directly from frozen. In that formulation, the inventors chiefly attribute the rise to chemical leavening and use yeast for flavor. That illustrates a manufacturing method; it does not establish the recipe used by every brand.

For a concrete supermarket example, DiGiorno’s rising-crust pepperoni ingredient list includes yeast, baking soda, added wheat gluten, and dough conditioners. The label alone cannot tell us its exact proofing process or how much each ingredient contributes.

To make a similar texture at home, start with a moderately thick, well-proofed pizza dough. Height and density are separate: a tall crust with plenty of gas cells can feel light and chewy. Bread flour helps the dough retain those cells and supports a puffy rim. King Arthur’s pizza guide
Here is a practical starting formula for one 12-inch/30-cm pizza; it is a home approximation:

on.li: 250 g bread flour
160 g water
5 g salt
5 g sugar
8 g oil
2 g instant yeast
Mix and knead until smooth and elastic. Cover and let rise until roughly doubled.
Gently stretch onto a lightly oiled pizza pan. Leave the outer ¾ inch/2 cm thicker, and preserve the bubbles there.
Cover and let the shaped dough become noticeably puffy, roughly 30–60 minutes depending on temperature.

Add a moderate amount of sauce and toppings. Bake in a fully preheated oven at 450°F/230°C, starting your checks around 15 minutes. The bottom should be browned and the dough beneath the toppings cooked through.

on.p: Adjust the dough quantity and final proof to tune the height. For a taller crust across the whole pizza, use a smaller pan; for a tall rim with a thinner middle, concentrate on shaping. King Arthur’s pizza-crust recipe demonstrates how the same dough produces several thicknesses through pan size and proofing.

Duplicating the freezer-to-oven performance is a separate challenge involving leavener timing, dough strength, and freezing conditions. For freshly made pizza, ordinary yeast dough gives you a useful route to the texture you describe.

off.p: Chef Joe, bake them uncovered at 400°F (200°C). Assuming they’re boneless, here’s a straightforward method:

off.li: Leave them whole. You don’t have to slice them thinner. If they’re exceptionally thick, you can cut each horizontally into two thinner cutlets; those will cook faster.
Use a shallow, oven-safe baking dish or a rimmed metal baking sheet, large enough to hold all three in one layer with a little space between them. Lightly oil it.
Lift the chicken out of the marinade, let excess drip off, and place it in the dish. Bake on the middle oven rack, uncovered.
Allow about 20–30 minutes for ordinary boneless breasts, or 30–40 minutes for very large, thick ones. Thin cutlets may take 15–20 minutes. Start checking at the shorter time.

Check each breast with a meat thermometer: the thickest center must reach 165°F (74°C) before you take it out. Insert the probe from the side into the center, avoiding bone. Time and color alone aren’t reliable measures of doneness. USDA guidance
Rest for 5 minutes before slicing.

off.p: If they’re bone-in, leave them intact and allow roughly 40–55 minutes, using the same temperature check. If the marinade starts getting too dark during baking, loosely cover the chicken with foil.

on.p: Chef Joe, bake them uncovered at 400°F (200°C). Assuming they’re boneless, skinless breasts, here’s a straightforward method:

on.li: Leave them whole. If they’re very thick, you can slice each horizontally into two thinner pieces for quicker, more even cooking.
Preheat the oven. Lightly oil an oven-safe baking dish or a rimmed metal baking sheet. Choose one large enough to hold all three breasts in a single layer with some space between them.
Lift the chicken out of the marinade, let excess liquid drip off, and put it in the dish.

Bake uncovered on the middle rack. Allow approximately 20–30 minutes for whole boneless breasts, or 15–20 minutes for thinner pieces. Very large breasts may take longer. Start checking at the early end of the range.

Check each breast with a meat thermometer. The thickest part must reach 165°F (74°C). Insert the probe into the center, avoiding bone if present. Time is an estimate; temperature determines when it’s ready. FoodSafety.gov
Rest for 5 minutes before slicing.

on.p: If they have bones, leave them whole and allow roughly 40–55 minutes at 400°F, checking for the same internal temperature. Betty Crocker’s bone-in breast recipe
Discard the leftover raw marinade. If you want to use it as a sauce, bring it to a full boil first. USDA marinade guidance

off.p: Strained bacon fat keeps for about 3–6 months in the fridge, in a tightly covered container. Your weekend batch should be fine for frying vegetables if you refrigerated it promptly and removed the bacon bits. Storage guidance.
The key distinction is fat versus mixed pan drippings:

table: Roast or other meat drippings containing juices, meat bits, or gelatin
Properly rendered, purified lard, tallow, or poultry fat
Longer than mixed drippings; follow product-specific guidance

off.p: For mixed drippings, I’d apply the USDA’s 3–4-day leftover limit. Solidifying in the fridge doesn’t make the meat juices underneath the fat keep longer. Proper rendering removes both moisture and impurities; simply straining roast drippings doesn’t necessarily do that. USDA leftovers guidance, Extension explanation.

Use a clean, dry spoon, label the jar with the date, and freeze small portions if you’ll use it slowly. Discard fat that develops mold or a rancid, sour, or paint-like smell—but don’t use a normal smell to extend the storage time of drippings containing meat juices. If you poured everything from the pan into the jar without separating it, use the shorter 3–4-day limit.

on.p: Strained bacon grease keeps for months in the fridge; meat drippings containing juices or meat bits should be used within 3–4 days. Keep the fridge at 40°F (4°C) or below.

on.li: Clean, strained bacon fat: A practical target is 3 months, stored in a clean, tightly covered jar. Published culinary guidance gives 3–6 months refrigerated. Bacon-fat storage guidance

Roast drippings, or grease containing meat bits or a watery/jelly layer: Treat these as cooked leftovers: 3–4 days refrigerated, or freeze promptly. This applies USDA’s guidance for cooked meat, gravy and broth to mixed drippings. USDA storage guidance

on.p: For your weekend jar, use the months-long window if you strained out the bacon bits and saved essentially just fat. If you poured everything into the jar, use the shorter window or freeze it in small portions.

For future batches, strain the warm fat into a clean, dry, heat-safe container, refrigerate promptly, date it, and use a clean spoon. Discard anything moldy or smelling rancid; normal smell does not establish safety. Perishable drippings should be refrigerated within two hours of cooking. FDA food-storage advice

off.p: A typical box of cake mix makes about 4 to 5½ cups of prepared batter, after adding the eggs, water, and oil. The exact yield varies with the brand, flavor, and box size; matching pan recommendations don’t guarantee identical batter volumes. Wilton’s guide

For your nonstandard pan, measure its capacity using water, then dry it before adding batter. For an ordinary cake pan, aim to fill it about halfway to two-thirds full, leaving room for the cake to rise. For example, a pan holding 8 cups of water to the brim would need roughly 4–5⅓ cups of batter. Wilton’s pan guide
For the most accurate planning, measure the prepared batter from your usual mix once and record its yield.

on.p: A typical box of cake mix makes about 4–5½ US cups of batter when prepared as directed. The exact yield varies by mix; that range comes from Wilton’s cake guide.
For your nonstandard pan, you can estimate the amount this way:

on.li: Use a measuring cup to fill the pan with water, counting the cups up to the rim.
Plan on batter equal to ½–⅔ of that capacity, leaving room for the cake to rise. Wilton recommends this fill level for ordinary cake pans.
Empty and dry the pan before adding batter.

on.p: For example, a pan holding 8 cups of water would need roughly 4–5⅓ cups of batter—about one box. For an exact yield from your favorite mix, measure one prepared batch and note it for future cakes.

off.p: Yes—very hot, especially boiling, water can contribute to cracking a natural-gourd or wooden mate cup. A mate-cup seller specifically warns about pouring hot water into dry wood; usual brewing water is around 70–80°C (158–176°F). Luv Mate’s care guide, Taragüi’s brewing instructions.

But heat cannot explain the first cup leaking during your cold-water soak. That suggests an existing crack, a thin or damaged area, or another defect. The other two could have failed because of excessive heat, pre-existing damage, or stresses as the material absorbed water; the timing alone doesn’t establish which.

Your day-long soak wasn’t an obviously unreasonable mistake: leaving yerba and water in the cup for about 24 hours is a conventional curing method, although instructions generally specify hot water. Wooden cups can require different preparation, so use instructions specific to the wood and maker. Taragüi’s curing guide.
For replacements:

off.li: Use warm water for initial wetting and avoid boiling water.
For calabash, scrape out softened loose pulp gently, without gouging the shell.
Empty after use and let dry with good airflow.

off.p: If you used water around 70–80°C, I would suspect the cups’ condition or quality before concluding that you caused all three failures. Curing won’t reliably repair a through-crack that leaks.

on.p: Yes—very hot water can contribute to cracking, especially in a wooden mate. Sudden changes in temperature and moisture are a concern: Almacén Argentino’s palo santo care guide specifically warns about these and advises warm water for curing, avoiding boiling water.
Your three failures need slightly different explanations:

on.li: The one that leaked during the cold-water soak: hot water cannot explain that failure if none had been added. A pre-existing crack or weakness is a plausible explanation.

The wooden one: excessively hot water could have contributed. The wood’s condition and preparation also matter; curing cannot reliably rescue an inherently weak vessel. Yerba Mate Lab discusses both water temperature and poor-quality wood as causes of cracking.

The natural calabash: leaving damp yerba inside for about a day is a common curing method. That step alone does not establish that you made a mistake. RioMates’ curing guidance uses hot, non-boiling water during the process.

on.p: For a replacement, follow instructions for its particular material. Wooden mates—especially palo santo—may have an oiling step before the damp-yerba treatment. Use warm water for curing, avoid pouring boiling water into the vessel, and let it dry naturally after use. For drinking, around 70–75°C (158–167°F) is a cautious starting point; this is practical guidance, not a guaranteed crack-prevention threshold.

Given that one leaked before its first hot-water use, there is good reason to suspect a defect in at least that one. For the other two, the actual water temperature and their condition before use would be needed to distinguish preparation damage from material defects.

off.p: Gnocchi are called dumplings because they are small, solid pieces of dough cooked as individual morsels. A dumpling doesn’t need a filling or a wrapper; plain dough dumplings count too.
The usual distinction is in their form and texture:

off.li: Noodles are typically dough stretched, rolled, or extruded into thin strands or strips.

Gnocchi are compact, relatively thick pieces of soft dough. Familiar potato gnocchi use cooked potato mixed with flour, giving them a tender, dumpling-like texture. Other versions use semolina or other ingredients, so potato alone isn’t what defines them. La Cucina Italiana

off.p: However, “technically a dumpling” makes the boundary sound stricter than it is. These are overlapping culinary categories, rather than a formal scientific classification. Gnocchi can also be grouped with pasta: the National Pasta Association describes them as “miniature pasta dumplings.” Share the Pasta
So *dumpling* describes their physical form well, while *pasta* can describe their broader culinary category. *Noodle* is usually a less fitting description of their shape.

on.p: Gnocchi fit the dumpling category because they are small, thick pieces of dough cooked as individual lumps. Typical potato gnocchi are made by mixing cooked potato with flour, shaping the dough into ropes, cutting off small pieces, and boiling them. That is a common way to make an unfilled dumpling. La Cucina Italiana describes them as dumplings.
The usual distinction is their form and preparation:

on.li: Noodles are generally dough formed into thin strands, ribbons, or sheets.
Dumplings are individual masses of dough, or dough enclosing a filling. A filling is optional; gnocchi belong to the unfilled kind.

on.p: Potato itself isn’t the deciding factor: gnocchi can also be made with semolina or other ingredients. Boiling doesn’t distinguish them either, since both noodles and dumplings can be boiled.

The word “technically” overstates how firm these categories are. Culinary terms overlap, and *pasta* is broader than *noodle*. Collins actually defines gnocchi as “pasta in the form of small, variously shaped dumplings.” Calling them dumplings is well established; calling them pasta can also be reasonable.

off.p: If the packaging is unclear, cook it before eating. “Smoked” does not necessarily mean “fully cooked” or “ready to eat”: bacon can be cured and smoked while still requiring cooking. USDA guidance
Some bacon is sold ready to eat, so it can be eaten without further cooking if the label or manufacturer confirms that. Smoking and curing alone aren’t enough to establish this.

It doesn’t specifically need grilling—frying or baking works too. For your package, follow any cooking instructions; if there are none, cook it or check with the manufacturer before eating it straight from the packet.

on.p: Cook it first unless the packaging or manufacturer confirms it is ready to eat. “Smoked” alone does not establish that bacon is fully cooked: smoking may leave it raw or partially cooked. Curing also does not guarantee it is safe to eat uncooked. USDA bacon safety guidance.

Bacon labelled “ready to eat,” “fully cooked,” or “precooked” can generally be eaten straight from the packet, provided you follow its storage instructions and use-by date. With your unclear label, treat it as requiring cooking until the manufacturer confirms otherwise.
Grilling is optional—you can fry, bake, or microwave it until thoroughly cooked.

off.p: The most likely explanation is sugar triggering bubble formation, followed by the coffee stabilizing those bubbles into foam.

Sugar crystals have tiny crevices and trapped air pockets that provide *nucleation sites*—places where bubbles can start growing. Heating reduces how much dissolved gas the liquid can hold, so adding sugar can help that gas escape as many small bubbles. If the coffee is near or above its boiling point, sugar can also trigger a brief burst of steam bubbles. Physicist Lou Bloomfield explains both mechanisms here.

Microwave heating can make this more noticeable because it heats the liquid directly, without the hot vessel surface that normally encourages bubbles to form during stovetop heating. A smooth glass can therefore leave bubble formation delayed until you add the sugar. The precise difference in your case depends on the temperatures and how much stirring or pouring each method involves. UNSW’s explanation of microwave heating and nucleation

The bubbles persist because coffee contains natural foam-stabilizing compounds, including protein-related substances, melanoidins and polysaccharides. These help keep bubble walls from breaking immediately. Their longevity suggests that the remaining bubbles contain air or other noncondensing gases: pure steam bubbles would disappear as the coffee cooled. Research on coffee’s foaming compounds
So the observation does not, by itself, prove superheating. Tiny persistent foam is consistent with gas release; sudden vigorous boiling when sugar is added would point more strongly to superheating.

on.p: The likely cause is sugar triggering the release of dissolved gas, followed by coffee stabilizing the bubbles into foam.

Hot water can hold less dissolved air than cold water. Rapid microwave heating can leave some excess air dissolved in the coffee. Sugar crystals provide nucleation sites—tiny surface irregularities where bubbles can start growing—so adding sugar releases many small bubbles at once. Cambridge’s explanation describes this effect.

The bubbles rise and collect at the surface. Coffee contains compounds that coat bubble surfaces and slow their merging and bursting, which explains the persistent layer. Experiments identify coffee’s polysaccharides as contributors to foam stability. Coffee foam study
Your heating-method difference likely reflects how much gas escapes during heating: slower heating, stirring, or boiling can release more of it before you add sugar.

If the coffee is near boiling, sugar can also trigger steam bubbles from superheated liquid. However, the foam lasting as the drink cools suggests that its bubbles contain gas such as air; steam condenses during cooling. Avoid overheating the coffee, since adding sugar to superheated liquid can cause sudden vigorous boiling. Study of microwave superheating

off.p: The most reliable fix is dilution: there isn’t a general-purpose ingredient that will cancel garlic’s sharpness without changing the pesto.
Since you’re out of basil, try adding:

off.li: More nuts and Parmesan, a little at a time. These increase the amount of pesto and balance the garlic with richer flavors.
Parsley or baby spinach, if available. They’ll dilute the garlic while keeping the sauce green, though they’ll change the flavor.
A little more olive oil, along with those additions. Too much oil alone will make the pesto greasy.

off.p: You can also use less pesto per serving and stretch it with pasta water, or mix it with ricotta for a milder, creamy sauce.
A small squeeze of lemon may improve the overall balance, but it won’t reliably remove the garlic bite; taste a spoonful with a few drops before adding it to the whole batch.
For your next batch, start with less raw garlic and taste before adding more. Blanching or roasting the garlic first will also give you a gentler flavor.

on.p: Dilution is the most dependable fix. There’s no general-purpose ingredient that reliably neutralizes raw garlic’s sharpness.
For your pesto, add a little at a time, then taste:

on.li: More pine nuts or walnuts: These increase the amount of pesto and soften the garlic’s impact.
More Parmesan: Helpful if the pesto can take additional salt.
A little more olive oil: Useful for adjusting consistency as you add nuts and cheese. Too much can make the pesto greasy.
Ricotta or cream: These dilute the garlic and give you a milder, creamy sauce.

on.p: You can also use less pesto per serving, tossing it with more pasta or vegetables. A spoonful of ricotta mixed into each portion is an easy way to rescue dinner.
Gentle cooking can mellow raw garlic, though heating the finished pesto will also change the basil’s fresh flavor. Lemon juice may improve the balance, but it won’t reliably remove the garlic burn.
For the next batch, start with a small amount of garlic and taste before adding more; individual cloves vary considerably in strength.

off.p: A very sharp, long slicing knife and well-chilled salmon are the usual approach. You can get paper-thin slices by hand; a mechanical slicer isn’t necessary.

First, the type of smoking matters: the silky, thin slices sold commercially are generally cold-smoked salmon. Hot-smoked salmon has a cooked, flaky texture, so it tends to break apart when sliced that thinly. Acme explains the difference.
For cold-smoked salmon:

off.li: Chill it thoroughly. If it still feels too soft, briefly put it in the freezer until firm but still flexible—start checking after about 15–20 minutes. You don’t need to freeze it solid. Tanner’s recommends this approach.
Leave the skin underneath on a stable cutting board and remove any remaining pin bones.
Use a long, narrow, very sharp knife, ideally a salmon slicing knife.

Hold the blade at a shallow angle, almost parallel to the surface, and shave off broad, thin slices with gentle, long drawing strokes. Use very little downward pressure; let the edge cut. Stop each slice before reaching the skin. Forman & Field’s carving guidance likewise recommends a sharp knife and smooth slicing strokes.

off.p: Your freezing idea is therefore useful as a firming step, but try hand slicing before freezing a whole side for a machine. Brief chilling makes the flesh easier to cut without requiring a full freeze-and-thaw cycle.

on.p: Use a very sharp, long, thin slicing knife and thoroughly chilled salmon. A flexible salmon knife is ideal.
For thin, broad slices:

on.li: Remove any pin bones and place the fillet skin-side down on a stable board.
Hold the blade at a shallow angle, almost parallel to the board.
Cut with long, gentle strokes, gradually shaving off a slice. Use very little downward pressure.
Stop just above the skin.

on.p: A salmon smoker’s carving guidance recommends a sharp blade and a smooth sawing action.

Your freezing idea is sound: partially freezing the fish firms it up for slicing. Start with refrigerator-cold salmon, then briefly put it in the freezer until firm but still yielding. Commercial processors sometimes chill smoked fillets to about −5°C before slicing, according to FAO processing guidance. For home use, try the knife method first; a powered slicer’s suitability depends on its blade and the firmness of the fish.

The smoking method matters, too. The silky, thin slices commonly sold are cured, cold-smoked salmon. Hot-smoked salmon is cooked and flakes more readily, so it is harder to achieve the same slices. Health Canada explains the difference.

Since you’re smoking fresh fish at home, use a validated curing and smoking procedure. Cold smoking can leave parasites alive; briefly firming the fish in the freezer for slicing does not constitute a parasite-control treatment. Food Standards Scotland provides guidance.

off.p: There isn’t a standard spoon-for-spoon conversion. Tender Quick can cure beef, but you should use a recipe formulated for it rather than replace the tablespoon of pink salt and subtract some kosher salt.

Assuming “pink salt” means Cure #1, it contains 6.25% sodium nitrite. Tender Quick is a different blend containing salt, sugar, sodium nitrite, and sodium nitrate. Its proportions and directions differ, so matching the saltiness alone won’t establish the correct cure dose. Oregon State Extension, Morton’s product guidance.

A concrete alternative is Morton’s deli-style corned beef cure: it specifies 5 tablespoons Tender Quick for a 4–6 lb brisket, with no additional kosher salt, applied as a dry rub with sugar and spices. It calls for refrigerated curing for five days per inch of thickness. That is a separate curing method—not a conversion for your original brine.

To assess your particular recipe, I’d need the meat weight, water quantity (if any), curing time, and ideally the recipe link. The two salt quantities alone aren’t enough to calculate a reliable substitution.

on.p: There’s no standard spoon-for-spoon conversion for replacing pink curing salt plus kosher salt with Tender Quick. The amounts you gave aren’t enough to calculate a safe substitution; the meat weight, water quantity, and curing method also matter.

Tender Quick contains salt and sugar, 0.5% sodium nitrite, and 0.5% sodium nitrate. Its formulation changes both the curing-agent dose and the salt content, so simply reducing the kosher salt won’t establish an equivalent cure. Morton’s product information
The practical approach is to use a curing recipe written specifically for Tender Quick. For example, Morton’s deli-style corned beef recipe uses:

on.li: 5 tablespoons Tender Quick for a 4–6 lb brisket, with sugar and spices and no additional kosher salt.
A dry rub, cured in a food-grade bag for 5 days per inch of meat thickness.

on.p: That quantity applies to Morton’s complete method; don’t use it as a replacement amount in your existing brine. Morton specifies keeping meat at 36–40°F (2–4°C) throughout curing and following the amount specified in the formulation. Morton’s curing directions
If you share the full pastrami recipe, including the brisket weight, water amount, and curing time, I can help assess a Tender Quick alternative.

off.p: Yes—your coworker is right that boiling and draining can produce perfectly good, fluffy rice. Think of cooking pasta: plenty of water doesn’t make it mushy provided you stop cooking when it’s done and drain it. The rice industry’s cooking guide explicitly describes this method as producing tender, separate grains. USA Rice cooking guide
There are three methods worth distinguishing:

off.li: Boiling and draining: Cook rice in plenty of water until tender, then drain. This tends to give separate, less sticky grains because some released starch leaves with the water.

Absorption cooking: Cook rice in a measured amount of water in a covered pot. The rice absorbs much of the water, and some evaporates. This is often called “steamed rice,” although the rice initially cooks directly in simmering water.
True steaming: Cook rice above boiling water so that steam supplies the heat, usually after soaking it.

off.p: The variety of rice matters greatly: sticky rice won’t become basmati simply because you drain it. With the same variety, both boiling and absorption can produce excellent results; draining generally favors loose grains, while absorption retains the starch and anything you’ve added to the cooking water.

To try it, rinse some basmati, add it to a large pan of boiling water, and start checking for tenderness around 10 minutes. Drain when ready, let it stand for about five minutes, then fluff. Tilda’s boiling method
Your concern applies if you add too much water and keep cooking until it all disappears. By then, the rice may be badly overcooked. Pouring off the excess changes the outcome.

on.p: Yes—your coworker is right that rice can be boiled in plenty of water, drained, and come out with tender, separate grains. It works much like cooking pasta: stop cooking when the rice reaches the texture you want, then drain it. Rice producer Tilda describes both this method and the absorption method.
The distinction is usually excess-water cooking versus absorption cooking:

on.li: Boil and drain: Cook in ample water, then discard the remaining liquid. Some released starch leaves with that water, which can help keep the grains separate.

Absorption cooking, often called “steaming”: Cook with a measured amount of water in a covered pot. The rice initially cooks in simmering water; it finishes and rests in the moist, steamy pot. The released starch stays with the rice.

on.p: True steaming means cooking rice above the water in a steamer; that is a third method.

Too much water alone doesn’t make rice into pudding. Cooking it long enough for the grains to soften and break down produces that result. With the drain method, you remove the water while the grains still have the texture you want. Rice variety also matters: basmati naturally produces more separate grains than sticky rice.

To try it, simmer basmati in a generous pot of water, taste periodically, and drain as soon as it is tender. Let it stand for about five minutes, then fluff it. You can get fluffy rice with either method; the amount of water mainly changes how you manage the cooking.

off.p: Separate the crushing from the chopping. Garlic and dried chillies benefit from becoming a paste; the herbs can stay as distinct, finely cut pieces. You then need only a quick stir to combine them.
For batches of 8–12 servings, I’d use this workflow:

off.li: Wash and thoroughly dry the herbs ahead of time. A salad spinner helps. Remove tough stems, but don’t spend time picking every tender parsley or coriander leaf individually.
Crush the chillies separately. Grind a small supply in a spice grinder, or crush one batch in a mortar before adding anything wet.
Make the garlic paste separately. A garlic press removes the slicing step; a fine rasp grater also produces paste that mixes readily into the dressing. Microplane’s blade guide

Chop the herbs in manageable handfuls. Gather them into a compact bundle, slice across it, then make a few crosswise passes with a very sharp chef’s knife. Repeatedly working a large, loose mound adds time and bruises the leaves.

Mix the garlic and chilli into your prepared liquid, then fold in the herbs. If you want some crushed-herb character, briefly pound a small portion of the herbs with the garlic, leaving the remainder chopped.

off.p: A mezzaluna—a curved, rocking herb knife—is worth considering if ordinary knife work is your main bottleneck. It can mince a mound of herbs while letting you control the endpoint; it’s used specifically for sauces such as salsa verde. It isn’t necessarily faster than a sharp chef’s knife in practised hands. Bon Appétit’s hands-on account
The biggest likely saving is eliminating the prolonged final crushing: get the garlic and spices to their finished texture first, and stop chopping the herbs as soon as they’re fine enough.

on.p: I’d separate the crushing from the herb chopping, and try a mezzaluna for the herbs. That gives you control over the texture at each stage.
For each batch of 8–12 servings:

on.li: Prepare the herbs ahead. Wash, spin dry thoroughly, remove tough stems, and refrigerate until needed. Leave the leaves whole until you make the sauce.

Crush the flavour base separately. Grind the dried chillies in a mortar, then add the garlic and some of your measured salt and work into a paste. A garlic press can eliminate the slicing step. Keep the oil and other liquids out until the grinding is finished.

Chop the herbs in manageable handfuls. Gather each handful into a compact bundle, slice finely across it, then make a short chopping pass across the slices. Stop at your preferred texture; repeatedly chasing the last large piece means working the whole pile again.

Combine and finish briefly. Stir the garlic–chilli paste into your liquid mixture, fold in the herbs, then give the sauce only as much final crushing as your preferred flavour and texture require. Finely chopped herbs can simply be stirred into salsa verde, as in Riverford’s method.

on.p: A mezzaluna is the curved, two-handled blade you rock across a board. It’s a useful option for repetitive herb chopping; Nigella describes the tool and its use here. I’d choose a sharp single-blade version for easy clearing and cleaning. Its speed advantage will depend on your knife skills, so borrowing one for a batch would be a useful trial.

The biggest practical saving is having dry, picked herbs ready to chop and a fully crushed garlic–chilli base ready to mix. If crushing the herbs contributes to the flavour you like, retain a brief finishing step and compare the result with your usual batch.

off.p: There is no universal minimum liquid level for slow cookers, and the meat does not need to be submerged. The amount depends on the recipe and your cooker’s instructions.

The “½ to ¾ full” advice refers to all the contents—food plus liquid. It helps recipes cook within their expected times; it does not mean filling half the pot with water. Crockpot’s guidance also explains that slow cookers lose very little water through evaporation.

For your turkey, use the ½ cup specified on the package, provided your cooker’s manual permits that recipe and roast size. A shallow layer is expected: the turkey releases juices as it cooks, and the covered pot retains moisture. USDA advises adding the amount of liquid specified in the recipe and checking the cooker’s manual for suitable meat sizes. USDA slow-cooker guidance

Start with the roast fully thawed, keep the lid on except for the instructed temperature checks, and follow your package’s cooking and temperature directions. Its 140°F check is an intermediate checkpoint, not the finished cooking temperature. USDA’s minimum safe final temperature for turkey is 165°F; your quoted package specifies 170°F. USDA turkey guidance

on.p: There is no universal minimum liquid level for slow cookers. Use the amount specified by the recipe and check your cooker’s manual for any model-specific requirements. USDA guidance says to add the amount of liquid suggested in the recipe. USDA slow-cooker guidance

The recommendation to keep a cooker half to three-quarters full refers to the total contents—food plus liquid, not the water level. It helps the cooker perform predictably within the recommended cooking time. Crock-Pot cooking tips

For your turkey, use the ½ cup of water specified on the package, provided your cooker matches the size described and its manual permits that method. The turkey releases juices as it cooks, and a covered slow cooker loses very little moisture through evaporation. The roast does not need to be submerged.

Start with the roast fully thawed, keep the lid on except for the instructed temperature checks, and follow the package’s four-hour checkpoint and final temperature. If your cooker is substantially larger than the specified 8-inch model, use a suitably sized cooker or the package’s oven method; adding water to reach three-quarters full would substantially change the recipe.

off.p: KitchenAid’s standard stand mixer attachments aren’t a good choice for making peanut butter. The two grinders have different limitations:

off.li: Grain mill: Don’t use it for peanuts. KitchenAid explicitly warns that their high oil content can damage the grinding mechanism. KitchenAid’s grain mill guidance

Food/meat grinder: It can grind nuts, but its blade and perforated plates produce ground pieces rather than the very fine, creamy paste you want. I wouldn’t buy one for peanut butter. KitchenAid’s grinding guidance

off.p: The hopper machine at your merchant is likely a dedicated nut butter mill. Its resemblance to a meat grinder doesn’t mean the grinding mechanism is equivalent.

For home use, a standalone food processor with an S-shaped blade is the practical option. Process roasted, shelled peanuts until they progress from crumbs to a clump and then a creamy paste, stopping to scrape the bowl as needed. KitchenAid recommends this method itself. Its stand mixer *food processor attachment* only slices, shreds, juliennes or dices; it lacks the blade needed for this task. Peanut butter instructions, attachment functions

on.p: KitchenAid’s grinding attachments aren’t a good choice for making smooth peanut butter.

on.li: Food grinder: It can grind nuts, but KitchenAid describes the result as mealy. Expect ground peanuts; don’t count on it producing a smooth, spreadable butter. KitchenAid’s food-grinder guidance.
Grain mill: Do not use it for peanuts. KitchenAid explicitly warns that their high oil content can damage the grinding mechanism. KitchenAid’s grain-mill manual.
Food processor attachment: This attachment slices, shreds and juliennes; it lacks the bowl and multipurpose blade needed to repeatedly process nuts into butter. Attachment features.

on.p: The hopper machine at your merchant is likely a dedicated nut-butter mill, designed to turn oily nuts into a paste. Machines of that kind are made specifically for shops selling freshly ground peanut butter. Nut-butter mill manufacturer.

For home use, choose a standalone food processor rated for nut butter. Add roasted, shelled peanuts and process until smooth, stopping to scrape the bowl as needed and following its operating limits. KitchenAid provides instructions for that method. Making peanut butter in a food processor.

off.p: The herbs and pepper are very unlikely to have supplied enough oil to keep 12 ounces of butterfat liquid. Your intuition about the quantities is sound. Poor straining might leave flecks or sediment, but it would not normally prevent the fat from setting.

The more likely explanation is delayed crystallization after melting. Butterfat contains a mixture of fats that crystallize at different temperatures. Fully melting it destroys its existing crystal structure; cooling it back to a temperature where solid butter normally holds its shape does not necessarily make it firm immediately. Cooling rate and time affect how those crystals reform. That makes crystallization a plausible explanation for your batch, although the exact temperature and cooling time would be needed to establish it. Research on butterfat crystallization

Try refrigerating a small portion for several hours, or overnight. It should become firm; then bring it back to kitchen temperature and see how it behaves. If it sets in the fridge, the problem was most likely its cooling history or temperature. If the fat itself remains liquid after overnight refrigeration, that would be unusual for clarified butter and would suggest substantial added liquid oil or a butter blend.
Fresh herbs can also introduce water. That may leave a separate liquid layer beneath the solidified fat, but it does not mean the butterfat failed to set.

on.p: The herb and pepper oils are very unlikely to explain it. Cooling and fat crystallization are the more plausible causes, although the cooling time and actual temperature would be needed to pin it down.

Your intuition about the quantities is sound: a handful of herbs contributes very little oil compared with 12 ounces of butterfat. For scale, a 2019 basil study measured just 0.02–0.17 grams of essential oil per 100 grams of fresh basil.

Butterfat sets by forming a network of fat crystals. Melting destroys that network, and rebuilding it takes time; its texture depends on both temperature and cooling history. A batch can therefore remain fluid at a temperature where previously set butter holds its shape. Clarified butter can also have solid grains suspended in liquid fat. Tetra Pak’s dairy handbook explains how crystallization governs butter’s consistency.

Refrigerate a small portion for several hours or overnight. The fat should become firm. If it does, that strongly supports a cooling/crystallization explanation. If a separate watery layer remains, the fresh ingredients may have introduced moisture that stayed behind.
Incomplete straining would explain flecks or cloudiness; ordinary amounts of leftover herb or milk solids would not keep the entire butterfat portion liquid.
For storage, treat this as a fresh herb infusion: refrigerate promptly and use within four days, or freeze. That follows university extension guidance for homemade herb-infused oils.

off.p: There’s no reliable arrowroot-to-carrageenan substitution ratio for nondairy cheese. Kappa carrageenan helps cheese set into a firm gel; arrowroot thickens the mixture, so substituting it may give you a soft spread or sauce rather than sliceable cheese. (Carrageenan properties, arrowroot uses)
For a firm cheese, use the carrageenan specified or a recipe designed for another setting agent, such as agar.
Could you share the recipe, including how much carrageenan it calls for? That will help determine whether an arrowroot adaptation is practical and how much to try.

on.p: There’s no reliable arrowroot-to-carrageenan substitution ratio for nondairy cheese. Arrowroot thickens the mixture; kappa carrageenan forms the gel that helps it set into sliceable cheese. Using arrowroot alone will give a different texture.

Agar-agar is a possible substitute for setting the cheese, though it changes the texture and melting behavior. This vegan cheese recipe uses arrowroot as a starch substitute and agar as a carrageenan substitute.
