off.p: Either clockwise or counterclockwise is fine when stirring chocolate by hand. There is no universal “correct” direction.

The process you probably remember is tempering, also called pre-crystallisation. It controls the crystal structure of cocoa butter so the chocolate sets with a glossy surface and a crisp snap. The key factors are temperature, time and movement; Callebaut’s instructions specify no stirring direction. Callebaut’s tempering guide

There is a possible explanation for your friend’s factory story: conching, an earlier manufacturing stage involving prolonged mechanical mixing. In some conches, reversing the motor changes how the asymmetrical mixing elements work, affecting shear, viscosity and removal of volatile acids. Direction therefore can matter for a particular machine and processing stage, without implying a rule for stirring a bowl. Research on conching direction
So tempering best matches the remembered shininess; conching could explain a factory-specific direction rule. I couldn’t verify the claim that reversing hand-stirring direction ruins a batch.

on.p: For hand stirring, either clockwise or counterclockwise is fine. The procedure you’re probably remembering is tempering, also called *pre-crystallisation*. It controls the cocoa butter’s crystal structure so the finished chocolate sets with a glossy surface and a firm snap. Callebaut identifies time, temperature and movement as the key factors; its instructions prescribe no stirring direction. Callebaut’s tempering guide

Your friend’s factory story could have involved a particular machine’s required rotation. For example, Cargill chocolate specialist Joe Sofia describes a tempering machine whose bowl turns clockwise against fixed scrapers. That arrangement mixes the chocolate and distributes cocoa butter crystals. Its direction follows the equipment’s design. Chocolate-Tempering Equipment and Techniques

Another possible term is conching, an earlier mixing and shearing stage. Industrial conches can use different rotation directions for different stages of processing. A study of industrial conching The reference to shine, though, points most strongly to tempering. Identifying the factory’s equipment would be necessary to establish which direction mattered in that particular case.

off.p: Thicken the sauce while it’s cooking; don’t wait for it to cool. For a cream-based Alfredo, the best first fix is to evaporate some water before adding the cheese.
Try this approach:

off.li: Use heavy cream. Milk or half-and-half will give you a thinner sauce with the same cooking time.
Simmer uncovered, stirring frequently, until the cream coats the back of a spoon. Judge by consistency rather than the recipe’s timer. As a useful benchmark, reduce 1½ cups of cream to about 1 cup.
Turn off the heat and gradually stir in finely grated Parmesan. Freshly grated cheese helps you get a smooth sauce. These steps are also used in Jessica Gavin’s Alfredo recipe.
Toss immediately with hot, well-drained fettuccine. If it becomes too thick, add reserved pasta water a tablespoon at a time. Serve promptly, preferably in warm bowls.

off.p: Reduction concentrates the flavor you already have; adding lots more cheese can make the sauce overly salty. Aim for a sauce that coats the noodles while hot—it will firm up a little more as you eat.
I couldn’t retrieve the linked recipe, so I can’t check its particular proportions.

on.p: Thicken the cream on the stove, then add the Parmesan and toss with hot pasta. Cooling can thicken Alfredo a little, but the sauce should already coat a spoon before you serve it.
For a cream-based Alfredo, try this:

on.li: Use heavy cream. Milk or half-and-half will produce a thinner sauce with the same quantities and cooking time.

Gently simmer the cream uncovered before adding cheese. Stir frequently, scraping the bottom. Judge by consistency: it should coat the back of a spoon. For reference, Jessica Gavin’s recipe reduces 1½ cups of heavy cream to about 1 cup.
Turn off the heat and stir in finely grated Parmesan. It adds thickness as well as flavor. Avoid a hard boil after adding cheese, which can make the sauce grainy or separate. Recipe and method
Add the hot, drained fettuccine and toss thoroughly. Keep reserved pasta water handy; add a tablespoon at a time only if the sauce becomes too thick. Serve immediately in warmed bowls.

on.p: Based on your description, insufficient reduction is a likely cause. If the sauce is smooth but milky, reduce the cream more next time. If it has oily puddles or cheese clumps, address the heat and cheese incorporation.

I couldn’t retrieve the linked recipe, so I can’t check its proportions. For preserving the flavor you already like, start by adjusting the reduction step; adding more cheese will also increase saltiness.

off.p: The most likely ingredient is Sichuan peppercorn, also spelled *Szechuan pepper* and called 花椒 (huājiāo).

Your “ants with hot feet” description fits its distinctive buzzing, prickling sensation remarkably well. Its active compound, hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, stimulates touch-sensitive nerves; researchers found that people compared the resulting tingle to a vibration of about 50 Hz. That explains why it feels like many tiny points of stimulation. Research on Sichuan pepper’s tingling
Combined with chillies, it produces málà (麻辣)—“numbing and spicy.” To find that experience again, look for Sichuan peppercorns or dishes described as *mala*. Mala seasoning

The restaurant could have been TamJai SamGor: its cartoon mascot and spicy noodle soups fit your clues, though that identification is tentative. Its menu includes a “Hot & Numbing” mala soup. Company prospectus

on.p: You very likely tasted Sichuan peppercorns, also spelled *Szechuan pepper* and called huājiāo (花椒) in Chinese. Your “ants with hot feet” description fits their characteristic prickly, buzzing sensation.

Their active compound, hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, stimulates sensory nerves involved in touch, producing tingling and numbness. That explains the tiny, distinct points of sensation you remember. Research on Sichuan pepper’s sensory effects
When combined with chilli, the seasoning is called málà (麻辣): *má* means numbing and *là* means spicy. To find that experience again, look for mala noodles or Sichuan peppercorn oil.
The restaurant could have been TamJai or TamJai SamGor, Hong Kong noodle chains that serve mala broth, though the décor clues aren’t enough to identify it confidently. Company prospectus

off.p: Clarified butter is used mainly for control over the sauce’s composition and consistency, rather than just taste.

Ordinary butter is roughly 80–82% fat, with most of the rest being water and a small amount of milk solids. Clarified butter is almost entirely fat. Using it lets you add the butterfat while controlling the water separately through the vinegar-and-wine reduction or a splash of water. That makes it easier to get a rich, predictable consistency.

Normal melted butter works too. Its extra water may make the béarnaise a little looser, and its milk solids can give it a slightly milkier flavour and more opaque appearance. Many recipes successfully use whole butter.

Clarification doesn’t make the finished sauce much more resistant to heat: overheating can still coagulate the egg yolks and break the emulsion. Clarified butter’s higher smoke point is useful for frying, but irrelevant at béarnaise temperatures.
So you can try melted whole butter in your recipe. Add it gradually, whisk well, and judge the consistency before adding any extra water.

on.p: You can make béarnaise with ordinary melted butter. Clarifying it mainly gives you control over the sauce’s fat-to-water ratio and changes its flavour and appearance.

Clarification removes water as well as milk solids, leaving almost pure butterfat. Béarnaise is an emulsion of tiny fat droplets suspended in a watery mixture, stabilised by egg yolk. Using clarified butter lets you adjust the butterfat and liquid separately. With whole butter, you introduce extra water, so the same weight can produce a thinner, less concentrated sauce.

The milk solids contribute a dairy flavour and a paler, more opaque appearance. Clarified butter gives the traditional glossy finish; which flavour you prefer is a matter of taste. RecipeTin Eats describes this appearance difference.

The higher smoke point has little relevance here: béarnaise needs gentle heat, and its yolks will overcook well before butter would scorch. Clarified butter still requires careful temperature control and gradual incorporation. Kenji López-Alt’s explanation and recipe cover those failure modes and use whole butter successfully.
For your recipe, try melted unsalted butter, whisk it in gradually, and judge the consistency before adding any optional water. Expect a slightly different texture and flavour.

off.p: Popcorn pops when the kernel reaches about 180°C (356°F), typically within a range of roughly 177–187°C. Water trapped inside builds pressure until the hull ruptures; the sudden release lets the softened starch expand into popcorn. In one experiment using an oven, 34% of kernels popped at 170°C, compared with 96% at 180°C. Popping-temperature study

Yes, a 250°C oven is hot enough. The important distinction is between the oven temperature and the temperature inside the kernel: the kernel takes time to heat up, and it should pop well before reaching 250°C.

A covered roasting pan can therefore work, but I would expect it to be less convenient and less consistent than a saucepan on the hob. In an oven, the popped corn remains exposed to heat while you wait for the remaining kernels, and it is harder to shake the pan or stop heating promptly. At 250°C, that gives you less margin before scorching. This is a practical inference from the heating method, rather than a result established by the temperature experiment.
If you want to try it:

off.li: Preheat the oven to about 190–200°C as a starting point.
Use a small batch of plain popcorn kernels in a single layer in an oven-safe metal pan, with plenty of room for expansion.
Cover with an oven-safe lid that contains the popcorn but allows steam to escape.
Listen closely and remove the pan when popping becomes infrequent; avoid waiting indefinitely for every kernel.

off.p: That is an experimental starting point, not a tested roasting-pan recipe. For reliably good popcorn, I’d use a covered saucepan with a little oil: it transfers heat efficiently and lets you shake the kernels and remove the pan quickly when popping slows. The Popcorn Board gives instructions for that method. Stovetop popcorn instructions

on.p: Popcorn typically pops when the kernel reaches about 180°C (356°F). Yes, a 250°C oven is hot enough, and kernels can pop in a covered roasting pan.

The temperature varies slightly between kernels. In a 2015 study, researchers heated popcorn in an oven: 34% of the kernels popped at 170°C, and 96% popped at 180°C. Earlier measurements put the popping temperature around 177–187°C. Popcorn: critical temperature, jump and sound
Inside each kernel, heat raises the pressure of its trapped moisture. When the hull ruptures, the sudden pressure drop lets the hot water expand into vapour, puffing up the softened starch.

The kernel temperature and oven setting are different things. The oven needs time to heat the pan and the kernels; setting it above 180°C helps them reach popping temperature faster. Research comparing heating in oil and air confirms that heat transfer affects how quickly kernels pop. Kinetics of Popping of Popcorn

For your roasting pan, I’d expect popping to work, but a stovetop pan is easier to control for a good batch. My practical concern with the oven is that early-popped pieces remain exposed to heat while the slower kernels finish. At 250°C, that gives you less margin before scorching.
If you want to experiment:

on.li: Start with a small batch in a fully preheated oven around 200°C; treat this as a starting point.
Use a roomy, oven-safe metal pan, with kernels in a single layer and plenty of space for expansion.
Cover with an oven-safe lid that allows some steam to escape.
Stay nearby and remove the pan promptly when popping slows substantially.

on.p: So: about 180°C inside the kernel; 250°C will work, but I’d start lower for an oven trial.

off.p: The dimples do more than give focaccia its characteristic appearance: they make little wells for olive oil. Oil pools there instead of simply running off, making those pockets softer and more flavorful. In focaccia recipes that use a saltwater brine, the dimples hold that too. Completely Delicious

Dimpling also locally compresses the dough and deflates some gas bubbles, helping control large bulges as it bakes. You still want plenty of air elsewhere, so use oiled fingertips and press deeply but gently—don’t flatten the whole dough. King Arthur’s focaccia instructions

on.p: Dimpling has practical purposes as well as giving focaccia its characteristic appearance.

The dimples make little reservoirs for olive oil and, in some recipes, salty water. These keep the topping spread across the bread and create flavorful, tender pockets in the surface. Baker Annalise Sandberg explains this effect here.

Pressing into the dough also breaks up some large gas bubbles, helping control uneven puffing during baking. The dough between the dimples still rises, so the finished bread remains airy. Bakers discuss this effect at The Fresh Loaf.

Use oiled fingertips and press deeply, while keeping the dough intact; you’re making wells, not piercing holes through it. King Arthur’s instructions describe pressing down to the pan without breaking through the dough.

off.p: Soy milk and sugar water are two evidence-backed vegan options for relieving chili-pepper burn.

off.li: Soy milk: Take a mouthful and swish it over the burning areas. A controlled study found that soy milks reduced capsaicin burn more effectively than water, with some evidence that higher protein content helped. Casein therefore isn’t essential for relief. Study on dairy and plant milks

Sugar water: Dissolve 20 g of sugar in enough water to make 100 mL, then rinse your mouth with it for about 15 seconds. That concentration and rinse time reduced burning more than plain water in a human study; relief developed over the following minutes. Sucrose rinse study

A sweet, noncarbonated fruit drink: This is a convenient alternative. A beverage comparison found that a fruit-flavored drink containing roughly 10% sugar reduced burn more effectively than water or seltzer. Beverage comparison

off.p: One correction to the premise: cold can help, even though it doesn’t chemically neutralize capsaicin. Experiments found cold rinses more effective than room-temperature ones. These options alleviate the burning sensation rather than instantly eliminating it. Temperature and rinse study

on.p: Soy milk and sugar water are evidence-backed vegan options for easing the burn from chili peppers.

on.li: Soy milk: Take a mouthful and swish it around the burning areas. A 2023 study by Gaiser and Hayes found that soy-milk rinses reduced capsaicin burn more effectively than water in its second experiment. Plant proteins can help; casein is one protein with this effect.

Sugar water: Dissolve 20 g of sugar in enough water to make 100 mL, then rinse your mouth with a mouthful for about 15 seconds and spit it out. A 2022 study found that this 20% sugar solution reduced burning more than plain water, with measurable relief within roughly a minute.
A sweet, still fruit drink: This is a convenient alternative. In a 2019 study of 72 people, fruit punch containing approximately 10% sugar was among the most effective drinks tested.

on.p: “Neutralize” is slightly misleading: these options reduce the burning sensation, and complete, immediate relief is not guaranteed. Water can provide some relief too—the 2019 study found that it helped—but several other drinks worked better.

off.p: Yes, oil type can affect an emulsion—but there is no general rule that sunflower oil emulsifies poorly. Your observation is plausible, although it could reflect the particular oils’ processing as much as their plant sources.

Whisking breaks oil into droplets; mustard helps keep those droplets from joining together again. Oil composition affects this process, including the small amounts of naturally occurring surface-active substances. A study comparing differently refined sunflower oils found that oils retaining more phospholipids had lower oil–water interfacial tension and formed stronger interfacial films. So two bottles labelled “sunflower oil” can behave differently. Study in *Food Hydrocolloids*

However, forming an emulsion and keeping it stable are separate questions. A controlled comparison of olive, rapeseed and sunflower oils found no significant difference in initial droplet size, but did find differences in separation during storage. Sunflower oil performed well in that experiment. These were laboratory emulsions using a different emulsifier and much stronger mixing than yours, so they do not establish a ranking for hand-whisked vinaigrette. Comparative study in *Foods*

If your olive, walnut and pumpkin seed oils are unrefined while your sunflower oil is refined, their retained minor constituents are a possible explanation, rather than a demonstrated diagnosis. Mustard quantity, oil-to-vinegar ratio and mixing also affect texture and stability. Mustard-vinaigrette study

For a neutral alternative, try refined canola/rapeseed oil. It has a mild flavour and is suitable for salad dressings; cold-pressed versions can have a more noticeable flavour. There is no guarantee it will emulsify better than your sunflower oil. Canola Council’s culinary guidance

A useful kitchen test is to split one vinegar–mustard mixture equally between two bowls, then add equal quantities of the two oils using the same whisking technique. Compare both the immediate texture and separation after 10–15 minutes. For more reliable results with either oil, whisk vigorously and add the first portion slowly, until the mixture looks uniform, before adding the rest.

on.p: Yes: oil type can affect how easily an emulsion forms, its texture, and how long it holds together. Your observation is plausible, though the evidence does not establish a general rule that sunflower oil emulsifies poorly.

Whisking breaks oil into droplets dispersed through the watery vinegar or lemon juice. The final texture depends on the size of those droplets, the proportion of oil, and how effectively the emulsifier keeps the droplets from joining together. Oil composition affects this process in two relevant ways:

on.li: Viscosity: oils differ in thickness, which affects how readily mixing breaks them into droplets. A thicker oil does not automatically produce a more stable emulsion.

Minor constituents: oils contain varying amounts of naturally surface-active substances, including phospholipids and mono- and diglycerides. These act at the boundary between oil and water and can affect emulsification. Processing and refining change their concentrations.

on.p: There is research close to your question: a 2011 study of differently processed sunflower oils examined how residual phospholipids affected emulsification and the stability of sauce-like emulsions. This supports the idea that the particular oil’s processing can matter, alongside its botanical source. Mezdour, Desplanques and Relkin, *Food Hydrocolloids*

The results also depend on the recipe and mixing method. In a 2022 comparison of olive, rapeseed and sunflower oils, oil choice significantly affected separation, but sunflower emulsions showed less creaming than refined rapeseed emulsions. Those experiments used a different emulsifier and intensive mechanical processing, so they cannot directly predict the behaviour of your hand-mixed Dijon vinaigrette. They do show why a universal ranking would be misleading. Kampa and colleagues, *Foods*

Refined canola oil—often sold as refined rapeseed oil—is a sensible neutral-flavoured alternative. Choose refined oil; cold-pressed rapeseed oil has a more noticeable flavour. The Canola Council describes refined canola as neutral-tasting and suitable for vinaigrettes. It is a practical substitute, with no guarantee that it will outperform your sunflower oil in this recipe. Canola Council

To check your observation, make two small batches with measured, identical quantities of vinegar and Dijon, using oils at the same temperature. Use the same whisk and mixing time, then compare both the initial texture and separation after ten minutes. For everyday preparation, a whisk and a slow initial addition of oil should make the result more consistent than stirring with a spoon or fork.

off.p: Too little water can produce a dry, crumbly loaf, but the more typical result is a dense, tight, firm crumb with reduced rise. Crumbliness alone doesn’t prove that the dough was underhydrated.

Water allows flour proteins to form gluten and makes the dough extensible enough to expand. With insufficient water, the dough is stiffer and fermentation is slower. With adequate water, it generally expands more readily and produces a moister crumb. However, low hydration can be intentional: bagels have firm dough and a tight, chewy interior without being crumbly. “Enough water” depends on the flour and bread style; wholemeal flour generally needs more than white flour. King Arthur’s guides to water and dough hydration.

Oven humidity mainly affects the crust and the loaf’s initial expansion. Steam keeps the surface flexible early in baking, allowing better oven spring; it also helps develop a glossy, crisp crust. Lack of steam is usually not the main explanation for a dry, crumbly interior, and adding steam cannot compensate for insufficient water in the dough. Soft sandwich bread can bake successfully without added steam. Guide to baking with steam.
For a soft, moist interior, focus on these factors:

off.li: Get the flour-to-liquid balance right. Weigh your ingredients and avoid adding lots of flour during kneading just to eliminate stickiness. For most soft sandwich breads, the dough should be supple and slightly tacky. Dry dough and unsoaked grains can contribute to crumbliness. Bread troubleshooting.

Choose a recipe designed for softness. Butter or oil makes the crumb more tender; enriched sandwich breads and rolls are better starting points than lean, crusty breads. Softness and moisture are related, but fat can improve tenderness without increasing water content. Bread ingredients and texture.

Develop the dough and allow adequate rising. Enough kneading or folding, followed by appropriate fermentation and proofing, produces a lighter interior. Extra water alone won’t guarantee that texture. Crumb development.

Bake until done, without unnecessarily extending the bake. Continued baking removes more moisture. Follow the recipe’s temperature and doneness guidance rather than trying to obtain a very dark crust on a soft loaf.

Consider tangzhong. Cooking a small portion of the recipe’s flour and liquid into a paste helps retain water, yielding soft bread that stays moist longer. Start with a tested tangzhong recipe. Tangzhong explained.

Store it well after cooling. Wrap soft bread airtight; freeze what you won’t eat soon. Refrigeration accelerates staling, which can make bread feel dry even without substantial moisture loss. Bread storage guide.

off.p: For a loaf that is dry immediately after cooling, check ingredient weights, flour added during handling, and baking duration first. If it starts soft and becomes dry later, storage and staling deserve more attention.

on.p: Too little water can produce a dry, crumbly interior, but its most characteristic effect is a stiff dough that yields a dense, tightly textured loaf with reduced rise. Crumbliness can also come from too much flour, too little fat, or overbaking. This assumes ordinary yeast bread made with wheat flour. King Arthur’s bread troubleshooting guide

Water hydrates the flour’s proteins and starches and enables fermentation. With sufficient water, the dough can stretch as gas bubbles expand. With too little, expansion becomes harder. The amount needed depends on the flour and bread style: a bagel dough is deliberately stiff, while ciabatta dough is quite wet. A low hydration percentage alone therefore doesn’t establish that a recipe is under-watered. Hydration explained

Oven humidity mainly affects the surface and the loaf’s expansion. Steam early in baking keeps the surface flexible, allowing more oven spring; it also helps produce a glossy, crisp crust. Insufficient steam can limit expansion, but adding steam cannot compensate for too little water in the dough. Many soft sandwich breads bake successfully with no added steam. Baking bread with steam
For a soft, moist interior, focus on these factors:

on.li: Measure flour and liquid accurately. Weigh them, and use extra flour sparingly during kneading. Higher-protein flour and whole grains can require more water. Follow the recipe’s description of dough consistency; stickiness alone is a poor reason to keep adding flour. Bread troubleshooting

Develop the dough and allow it to rise adequately. Kneading or folding builds the gluten structure that holds gas, helping produce a lighter interior. Follow the recipe’s dough cues as well as its timings. Gluten development and crumb
Choose an enriched recipe for tenderness. Oil or butter makes the crumb softer. Moistness and tenderness are related, but fat can improve tenderness independently of adding water. Ingredient effects

Consider a tangzhong recipe. Cooking a small portion of the flour with liquid before mixing the dough helps retain moisture and keeps the finished bread soft longer. Start with a recipe designed for the method. Tangzhong explained
Avoid overbaking. Extended baking removes more water and can make sandwich bread particularly crumbly. Use the recipe’s temperature, time, and doneness cues. How baking affects the crumb
Store it to retain moisture. Once cooled, wrap soft bread airtight. Freeze portions for longer storage; refrigeration accelerates staling. Bread storage guide

on.p: For troubleshooting, the timing helps: bread that is dry immediately after cooling points toward the recipe or baking; bread that starts soft and becomes dry later points toward storage and staling.

off.p: Further simmering won’t reliably make it milder, and evaporation can make the heat more concentrated. The beans may absorb some seasoning, spreading the heat more evenly, but they won’t remove it. Seasoned Advice

For your curry, the most dependable fix is to add more beans, tomatoes and cooked onion without adding chilli. Another tin of drained cannellini beans is a good start; simmer briefly, then taste. Adding beans is also recommended in the Bean Institute’s cookbook.
You can also stir in coconut milk or cream, or serve with plain yoghurt and rice to soften the perceived heat. Add yoghurt off the heat to help prevent curdling. Seasoned Advice

on.p: Extra simmering won’t reliably make it milder. Chilli’s heat comes from capsaicin, which survives ordinary cooking fairly well. Some breaks down with prolonged heating, but evaporation can concentrate the sauce and make it taste hotter. (Research on capsaicin during cooking)
The beans can take on the seasoned sauce, so the heat may become more evenly spread through each mouthful. They won’t neutralise it.

For your curry, add more drained cannellini beans and tomatoes, then simmer briefly and taste. Adding more unspiced ingredients is the most dependable fix; the Bean Institute’s cookbook specifically recommends extra cooked beans for an overly hot dish.
Coconut milk would also suit the curry and help soften the heat. You could serve it with plain rice and a spoonful of yoghurt, too.

off.p: “Chewy” can mean two different things, and the distinction matters:

off.li: A firm or chalky center: The rice hasn’t hydrated and cooked all the way through. Too little water, a leaking lid, or heat high enough to boil the water away before the grains soften can cause this.

A soft grain that’s still springy or sticky: That may be the rice itself. Glutinous rice is naturally chewy, and short-grain varieties tend to have more bite than fluffy long-grain rice. Brown rice also retains some chew from its bran layer.

off.p: Adding water and cooking longer helps the first problem, but won’t necessarily change the second. It can simply make the outside mushy while the rice still has its characteristic texture.
For more consistent rice:

off.li: Use the instructions for your particular variety. Water requirements differ, and the pot and lid affect how much evaporates.
Rinse ordinary white rice to remove loose surface starch. This reduces gumminess, though it won’t fix a hard center.
Cook covered at a gentle simmer, with a tight-fitting lid. Avoid frequent lifting of the lid or stirring.
Rest it off the heat, still covered, for 10–15 minutes. This lets moisture redistribute and finishes softening the grains.
Try soaking before cooking if the grains repeatedly have hard centers, especially with brown rice. Follow the variety’s guidance and account for water absorbed during soaking.

off.p: To rescue rice with hard centers, sprinkle in a little boiling water, cover tightly, and cook on very low heat for several minutes, then let it rest covered. If the grains are already fully soft but remain elastic, choosing a different rice variety is more likely to help than adding more water.

on.p: A hard or chalky center usually means the rice is undercooked. Rice needs moisture and sustained heat to soften throughout. Too little water, steam escaping from the lid, or water boiling away too quickly can leave the middle hard. Extra cooking time helps only while enough moisture remains. USA Rice’s cooking guide
To prevent it:

on.li: Follow the directions for your particular rice. Brown rice takes substantially longer than white rice, and water requirements vary.
Bring it to a boil, then cover tightly and reduce to a gentle simmer. Keep the lid closed during cooking.
After cooking, let it rest covered for about 10 minutes before fluffing.

on.p: To rescue a dry batch: add about 2 tablespoons of water per cup of rice originally used, cover tightly, and heat very gently for 5–10 minutes. Then let it rest covered. If there is already water in the pot, continue the covered simmer. Rouxbe’s troubleshooting guide

If the grains are fully cooked but springy or firm throughout, the rice type may explain why more water and time have little effect. Short-grain rice has some springiness, and parboiled rice stays firmer than ordinary white rice. Jasmine typically cooks soft and moist. USA Rice’s variety guide
What kind of rice are you using, and are you cooking it on the stove or in a rice cooker?

off.p: I’d freeze the dough now and bake the day before the party, assuming you’ll have enough oven time. That’s my recommendation for the freshest aroma and texture; all three of your cookie types are good candidates. Baking now and freezing is also a sound choice if spreading out the baking matters more.
For freezing the dough:

off.li: Portion it first, freeze the portions on a lined tray until firm, then transfer to airtight freezer bags. Label each with the baking temperature and time.
Chocolate chip: Bake from frozen at the usual temperature, allowing perhaps an extra minute or two.
Peanut butter: If your recipe calls for flattening with a fork, do that before freezing.

Snickerdoodles: Freeze the balls without cinnamon sugar. Before baking, let them soften just enough for the coating to stick, then roll and bake. Sally’s freezing guide specifically recommends this approach for coated cookies.

off.p: Bake a couple of frozen portions as a trial before committing the whole batch: freezing can affect spread, and the test will establish your timing. King Arthur’s guidance supports baking portioned dough directly from frozen.

If you’d prefer to finish the baking now, cool the cookies completely, pack airtight with parchment between layers, and freeze promptly. Thaw them still covered at room temperature for the party. Six days is comfortably within the recommended freezer storage period. Betty Crocker explains the packing method; Sally’s guide recommends covered thawing.
For standard versions of these recipes, you don’t need to provide more details.

on.p: I’d freeze the dough now and bake the day before, provided you’ll have time for all the batches. That’s my recommendation for freshness: the cookies get their final bake close to serving. Baking now and freezing the finished cookies is also a good option if you need to spread out the oven work. King Arthur’s make-ahead guide supports both approaches.
Standard snickerdoodle, peanut butter, and chocolate chip doughs are suitable for freezing. Here’s how I’d prepare them:

on.li: Chocolate chip: Scoop individual portions, freeze on a tray until firm, then transfer to an airtight freezer bag. Bake from frozen at the recipe’s temperature; they may need an extra minute or two.
Snickerdoodles: Freeze the portioned balls before adding cinnamon sugar. On baking day, let them soften for about 30 minutes so the coating sticks, then roll and bake.
Peanut butter: Shape before freezing, including the fork marks if your recipe calls for flattening. If you freeze them as balls, let them soften enough to flatten before baking.

on.p: Follow any chilling step in your recipe before freezing. These methods are covered in Sally’s freezing guide and King Arthur’s freeze-and-bake tips. Bake a few test cookies first to check timing and spread before committing a whole tray.

If getting the baking finished now matters more, cool the cookies completely, then freeze them in airtight containers with parchment between layers. Thaw them in the closed containers at room temperature. Six days is comfortably within Sally’s recommended freezer storage period of up to three months. Instructions for freezing baked cookies.
For a large party, a mix of the two methods is practical: bake and freeze some batches now, and save some dough to bake Friday.

off.p: The trick is to scoop up the bulk first, then wipe away the residue. A rag tends to push chunks around and quickly gets overloaded.

off.li: Scrape and scoop. Use a dustpan and a silicone spatula, plastic scraper, or two pieces of stiff cardboard. Push the food onto the dustpan and empty it into the trash. A spoon works well for smaller piles.
Blot the remaining liquid. Use paper towels or an old absorbent towel. For something especially soupy, scoop as much liquid as you can into a bowl first.
Wash and dry. Wipe with a cloth dampened with warm water and a little dish soap, then wipe with clean water and dry so the floor isn’t slippery.

off.p: For salsa under the fridge, slide a thin plastic scraper or stiff cardboard underneath and draw the chunks toward you. Then wrap a damp cloth around a flat ruler or yardstick to reach the residue. Secure the cloth so it doesn’t get left underneath, and avoid pushing food farther back. If you can’t reach everything, moving the fridge enough to clean underneath is the best way to prevent lingering smells.
For future spills, a cheap dustpan reserved for kitchen messes is surprisingly useful.

on.p: Scoop up the chunks, blot the liquid, then wash the floor. A dustpan and a flexible plastic scraper work well for salsa, stew, and soggy cereal.

on.li: Collect the bulk. Hold the dustpan flat against the floor and gently push the food into it with the scraper. Two pieces of stiff cardboard also work: use one as a scoop and the other as a pusher. Empty everything into the trash.
Absorb the liquid. Lay paper towels or an old towel over what remains, press down, and lift. Work from the edges toward the center to contain the spill.
Clean the residue. Wipe with a damp cloth and a cleaner suitable for your flooring, then dry the area. Avoid flooding seams in wood or laminate.

on.p: Under the fridge, a thin cloth wrapped securely around a flat ruler can reach a shallow spill. Draw it toward you gently so you bring the food out. For a large spill farther underneath, pull the fridge forward according to its manual, watching the power cord and any water line. Unplug it before cleaning underneath; GE’s cleaning guidance recommends this precaution.
If the container broke, collect the glass before handling the food, and use tools and gloves for the sharp pieces.

off.p: Yes—a sous vide circulator can slow-cook food in a second vessel inside its water bath. Your bain-marie idea is sound. The main limitations are temperature, heat transfer, and capacity.
For that setup:

off.li: Use a heat-safe inner container, preferably metal, supported so it cannot tip or float.
Have the bath water reach roughly the food’s level, while keeping it out of the inner container.
Leave room around the container for water circulation, and respect the circulator’s minimum and maximum water levels.
Cover the food and, where practical, the bath to reduce evaporation.

off.p: The temperature determines which recipes will work. The food can only approach the bath temperature, and a large bowl of thick stew will heat more slowly than a thin sous vide bag. A bath around 85–90°C can produce braised meat and cook many vegetables, but ordinary slow-cooker timings may need adjusting. Baldwin describes braised meat textures at 80–85°C; some circulators, such as the Anova Precision Cooker, top out at 92°C. You therefore cannot count on this setup to boil food or reduce a sauce substantially. Baldwin’s cooking guide, Anova specifications

For meat cooked at lower temperatures, use an established sous vide recipe with appropriate heating and pasteurization times. The bath reading does not tell you how quickly the centre of a bowl has heated. Baldwin’s safety and heating guide

Energy use need not be unreasonable. Heating the extra water takes energy initially; after that, consumption mostly depends on heat escaping through the container and evaporation. A covered, suitably insulated bath helps. The circulator’s advertised wattage is its maximum power, not necessarily its continuous consumption.
For inexpensive equipment, the choices are:

off.li: If you buy the circulator anyway: use an existing pot plus an inner bowl—or put the food and cooking liquid directly in a suitable sous vide bag. That is the cheapest additional setup.
If you want conventional slow cooking frequently: compare a basic slow cooker plus a budget circulator against a combined appliance. Two inexpensive devices may cost less and offer more flexibility.

If you want one appliance: choose a model explicitly offering both slow cooking and sous vide. Examples include Hamilton Beach’s Temp Tracker and certain Instant Pot multicookers; check the exact model’s functions. Hamilton Beach manual, Instant Pot example

off.p: There is no universal cheapest purchase without local prices, but your proposed bain-marie is a workable way to get both methods from a circulator, provided you adapt recipes to its temperature limits.

on.p: Yes—a sous vide circulator can heat a bain-marie containing a second bowl or pot. That arrangement can cook stews, braises and other dishes slowly. The main limits are temperature, heating time and container size.

Use a heatproof inner container, preferably stainless steel, with a lid. Keep the surrounding water roughly level with the food inside, while preventing water from entering the container. Leave room for water to circulate and keep the machine within its marked water-level limits. The circulator belongs in the clean outer water bath.
There are a few practical differences from a slow cooker:

on.li: Temperature: The food inside approaches the bath temperature gradually. Slow-cooker recipes often assume temperatures close to simmering; Crock-Pot says some of its models stabilize around 98°C/209°F. Check the circulator’s maximum temperature before buying. A lower setting can substantially lengthen cooking, especially for vegetables. Crock-Pot temperature information

Heating time: A large bowl of thick stew heats more slowly than a thin sous vide bag. Standard sous vide timing tables therefore won’t directly apply. For a stew, bringing it to cooking temperature on the stove before transferring it to the preheated bath makes the process more predictable. Sous vide safety depends on both temperature and time throughout the food. Douglas Baldwin’s cooking guide
Evaporation: Cover the bath during long cooks and monitor its water level. Sauces in a covered inner pot will reduce very little.

on.p: Energy consumption needn’t be unreasonable. The heater cycles to maintain temperature; its rated wattage is its maximum power, not necessarily its continuous consumption. An open bath near boiling loses considerable heat through evaporation. A covered, appropriately insulated bath reduces those losses. The extra water also requires energy during initial heating. Actual consumption depends on the setup; a plug-in energy meter can measure it.
For equipment cost:

on.li: If you buy the circulator anyway, using existing pots for the bain-marie could mean no additional equipment cost.
If you want conventional slow-cooker convenience too, compare a basic slow cooker plus an inexpensive circulator with a combined appliance.
Combined models exist: Crock-Pot sells slow cookers with a dedicated sous vide mode.

on.p: The cheapest purchase depends on local prices and what you already own. For the setup you describe, the bain-marie is a workable starting point.

off.p: Yes—if you mean dry, uncooked quinoa, rice, lentils, barley, farro, kasha and black beans, keeping them in the fridge is fine. With regular rotation, your method is reasonable.

Refrigeration itself doesn’t cause meaningful nutritional loss. Cold storage can help preserve freshness, especially in whole grains such as brown rice, whose natural oils can become rancid. Iowa State Extension recommends refrigerated or frozen storage for whole grains.
For dry foods:

off.li: Use airtight, moisture-resistant containers or tightly sealed bags.
Keep the contents dry, and use a dry scoop.
Avoid repeatedly leaving cold containers open in warm, humid air, which can introduce condensation.

off.p: White rice, dried lentils and beans also keep well in a cool, dry pantry, so refrigeration is optional. Utah State Extension

If you mean cooked grains or beans: refrigerate within two hours in shallow containers, keep the fridge at 40°F/4°C or below, and use within 3–4 days or freeze. Regular rotation doesn’t extend that storage window. USDA guidance

on.p: Yes—if you mean dry, uncooked foods, all of those can be stored in the fridge. Refrigeration helps preserve whole grains by slowing rancidity in their natural oils. Your regular rotation is a useful habit. Iowa State University Extension

You shouldn’t expect meaningful nutritional loss from refrigeration during normal storage. Cool storage slows vitamin breakdown; keeping the foods dry and properly sealed helps preserve their quality. Utah State University Extension
For dry grains, lentils and beans:

on.li: Use airtight, moisture-proof containers or well-sealed bags.
Keep containers and scoops dry. Moisture can allow mold to grow.
If moving a cold container into pantry storage, let it reach room temperature while sealed to limit condensation inside.

on.p: If you mean cooked grains or beans, refrigerate promptly in shallow containers, within two hours of cooking. Keep the fridge at 40°F/4°C or below, and use them within 3–4 days or freeze portions for later. These handling steps are especially important for cooked rice. USDA leftovers guidance, FoodSafety.gov

off.p: Yes—a temporary increase in perceived saltiness can happen after Sichuan pepper. Researchers have found that it can make salty foods taste saltier, and other people have reported a similar lingering “salty tongue” effect. Those anecdotes match your description, although studies of saltiness enhancement don’t fully explain why *everything* afterward would taste salty. Sensory study

A different batch or a larger amount is a plausible explanation. Sichuan pepper’s sanshools produce the familiar buzzing by stimulating sensory nerves; their concentration and composition vary between products. That could change the intensity of your experience, but it doesn’t identify the cause in your particular packet. Also check whether the ingredients include added salt or other seasonings. Sanshool mechanism, product variability study

A brief effect that wears off completely does not, by itself, suggest permanent taste-bud damage. However, the sensory studies aren’t proof that this particular batch is safe, and taste alone cannot establish or rule out contamination.

Since this is new for you, I’d pause this packet until your taste returns to normal. Check its ingredients, packaging, and any unusual odor or visible spoilage. If everything looks normal and you have no other symptoms, using a smaller culinary amount from a trusted source is a reasonable next step.

If the salty taste persists into the next day, occurs without eating the pepper, or comes with mouth pain or sores, stop using it and consult a doctor or dentist. Persistent salty taste can have other causes. Tongue or throat swelling, trouble swallowing, or breathing difficulty needs urgent medical care. NIDCD taste-disorder guidance, NHS allergy guidance

on.p: Yes—temporary extra saltiness is a plausible effect of Sichuan peppercorns, and other people have reported the same experience. Those reports are anecdotal, but a 2020 study involving 68 participants found that Sichuan pepper extract enhanced perceived saltiness, with effects varying by concentration and individual sensitivity. That supports an explanation for your experience, although it doesn’t establish how common a lingering salty tongue is.

A different batch or a larger amount could plausibly explain the change. Check the ingredients for added salt or seasoning, too. The sensation alone cannot tell you whether the peppercorns are contaminated.

Regarding permanent damage: sanshool, the compound responsible for the buzzing sensation, acts on sensory nerves; its effects were reversible in laboratory experiments. A brief effect that fully resolves is reassuring. However, those experiments don’t prove that every product or dose is safe, and the saltiness studies weren’t designed to assess long-term taste-bud damage.

For now, pause this batch until your taste returns to normal. If the package appears sound and you have only a temporary taste change, using a smaller culinary amount is a reasonable next step. Replace the batch if its ingredients or condition concern you.

If the salty taste remains into the next day, occurs when you haven’t eaten peppercorns, or comes with pain or sores, stop using them and contact a doctor or dentist; persistent altered taste merits assessment. Sudden tongue or throat swelling or trouble breathing requires emergency help.

off.p: I’d freeze it, mostly as plain leaves in small portions. That gives you the most flexibility later. Freezing papalo leaves is recommended by Chef Jeff’s Garden, although I didn’t find controlled comparisons showing which freezing method preserves papalo’s flavor best.
Here’s how I’d handle your harvest:

off.li: Pick healthy leaves, remove the stems, rinse under running water, and gently pat dry.
Divide into portions you’ll use at one time. Wrap each portion tightly in freezer wrap, then put the portions in a freezer bag and press out excess air.
Label with the date and freeze promptly.

off.p: This follows the National Center for Home Food Preservation’s method for fresh herbs. Expect the leaves to become limp after thawing—they’ll work better as chopped seasoning than as an attractive fresh garnish.

If you commonly use papalo in sauces or dressings, freeze some as herb-and-oil cubes instead: chop the washed, dried leaves, mix with enough olive or neutral oil to bind them, portion into an ice-cube tray, and freeze immediately. Transfer the frozen portions to an airtight freezer container. This is an established general method for herbs, rather than a papalo-specific tested recipe. Fresh herbs in oil must stay refrigerated or frozen because of botulism risk; thaw portions in the refrigerator and use within four days. Oregon State Extension

For storage, keep your freezer at 0°F / −18°C or below. Plan to use most of your harvest this winter: general herb guidance says quality can begin declining after 3–6 months, though frozen herbs can be kept for use within a year. Those are general estimates, not a verified papalo flavor lifespan. University of Georgia Extension, University of Minnesota Extension
Before processing everything, I’d freeze one small portion plain and one in oil, then taste both after a few days. That will let you choose based on how you actually eat papalo.

on.p: I’d choose freezing, in small portions. University of Illinois Extension specifically lists papalo among the herbs best preserved this way. Expect softer leaves after thawing; freezing preserves a usable seasoning, but the fresh garnish texture will change. (Illinois Extension, Penn State Extension)
For your harvest, I’d start with whole leaves frozen plain:

on.li: Pick healthy leaves, remove the stems, rinse under running water, and gently pat or spin dry.
Spread the leaves in a single layer on a baking sheet and freeze.
Once frozen, promptly transfer them to freezer bags. Press out excess air, seal, and label with the date.
Take out only what you need and keep the rest frozen. (Maryland Extension)

on.p: This gives you flexibility when using papalo in different dishes. My suggestion is to freeze a small test batch first, then taste it in your usual salsa or other dish a few days later before committing the whole harvest.

Freezing chopped papalo in oil is another useful option if oil suits your recipes. Apply Penn State’s general herb method: mix 2 cups chopped leaves with ⅓–½ cup oil, portion into small freezer containers or ice-cube trays, and freeze immediately. Transfer frozen portions to a sealed freezer container. A neutral oil lets the herb’s flavor dominate. This recipe is general herb guidance; it isn’t a papalo-specific flavor study. Keep the mixture frozen; fresh herbs in oil should never be stored at room temperature. (Penn State Extension)

For winter and some of next year, keep it at 0°F / −18°C or colder and plan to use it within one year. That is Minnesota Extension’s general recommendation for frozen herbs; papalo’s flavor may fade sooner. Good packaging and small portions will help you avoid repeatedly thawing the supply. (Maryland Extension, Minnesota Extension)

off.p: The handle could plausibly be aggravating your eczema, but that does not establish an allergy to Fibrox. I didn’t find a documented Fibrox-specific dermatitis problem in the sources I searched.

Victorinox identifies current Fibrox handles as thermoplastic elastomer (TPE)—a family of rubber-like synthetic materials. That description does not identify every ingredient or establish the composition of your decades-old handles. Victorinox product specifications
Two explanations are plausible:

off.li: Irritant contact dermatitis: friction from the textured grip, pressure, sweat, or cleaning residues could aggravate already vulnerable skin. The two contact spots you describe fit this possibility. Friction, sweating, and detergents are recognised eczema triggers. DermNet

Allergic contact dermatitis: you could be reacting to an ingredient in the handle or something deposited on it. Rubber-manufacturing chemicals can cause delayed eczema, including from handgrips—but that does not mean those chemicals are present in Fibrox. DermNet

off.p: Your latex intolerance does not settle the question. Allergy to natural-latex proteins and delayed allergy to manufacturing chemicals are different reactions; a rubber-like feel alone does not imply latex exposure. DermNet’s latex explanation

The improvement after switching knives is a useful clue, although three or four days cannot distinguish allergy, friction, and ordinary eczema fluctuation. Keep using the handles you tolerate, and bring this observation to your dermatologist. Ask about patch testing, which investigates delayed contact allergy rather than the immediate reactions assessed by skin-prick testing. Photos, knife model numbers, and information from Victorinox about the particular handle formulation could help guide testing. American Academy of Dermatology
Discuss the improvement with your prescriber before changing your corticosteroid schedule.

on.p: The handle is a plausible trigger, but your observation cannot yet distinguish an allergy from irritation. The rash’s location and improvement after changing knives are useful clues. I couldn’t find a published report specifically identifying Victorinox Fibrox handles as a cause of dermatitis.

Victorinox lists current Fibrox handles as thermoplastic elastomers (TPE). That describes a family of materials; the specification does not disclose the complete formulation or establish what is in your older handles. Victorinox product specification
Two explanations are worth investigating:

on.li: Irritant contact dermatitis. Friction from the textured grip, combined with sweat or detergent exposure, could aggravate existing eczema at those contact points. People with atopic eczema are particularly susceptible to irritation. DermNet: irritant contact dermatitis

Allergic contact dermatitis. A handle ingredient or substance on its surface could be responsible. Contact allergy can develop after years of exposure, so your long history with these knives does not exclude it. The exact substance would need investigation. DermNet: allergic contact dermatitis

on.p: Your latex intolerance is relevant history, but it does not establish an allergy to TPE. Immediate natural-latex allergy usually involves latex proteins; delayed eczema associated with rubber products often involves manufacturing chemicals. There is no evidence here that your handles contain those particular chemicals. DermNet: latex allergy

For now, keep using the handles your skin tolerates and photograph the improvement. Arrange a dermatology review and ask about patch testing, which investigates delayed contact allergy. Bring the knife’s model information and photos; the dermatologist can decide whether testing handle material would help. Patch testing does not diagnose friction-related irritation. DermNet: patch tests

Also ask Victorinox for the material and additive information for your specific models, mentioning your suspected contact dermatitis and latex history. Avoid deliberately provoking another flare, and discuss any change to your prescribed corticosteroid schedule with your clinician.

off.p: Wash them gently with dish soap and warm water, dry thoroughly, and switch to food-grade mineral oil for future care. One application of olive oil is not a reason to discard the utensils.

Olive oil *can* become rancid; that does not mean the oil you just applied already is. The reason to avoid it as a wood treatment is that it can eventually become sticky and develop unpleasant smells and tastes. University of Maine Extension recommends food-safe mineral oil instead.
Here’s what I would do:

off.li: Wipe off any excess oil with a clean cloth or paper towel.
Hand-wash briefly with warm water and ordinary dishwashing detergent, using a soft sponge or cloth. Rinse well. If the surface still feels greasy, repeat a gentle wash.
Towel-dry immediately, then let the utensils air-dry completely, with air circulating around them.
Once dry and free of objectionable odor, apply a light coat of food-grade mineral oil intended for cutting boards or utensils, following its instructions and wiping off excess.

off.p: Your concern about wood damage is reasonable, but brief washing is normal care for wooden utensils. Prolonged soaking, dishwashers, and leaving the wood wet are the bigger problems; aggressive scrubbing is unnecessary. The University of Minnesota’s guidance specifically for wooden kitchenware recommends washing in warm sudsy water without soaking.

There is a limitation: washing removes surface oil, but cannot guarantee extraction of all oil absorbed deeper in the wood. My practical recommendation is to clean it normally rather than attempt complete stripping. Mineral oil will not neutralize any olive oil that remains. If an unpleasant rancid odor persists or returns after washing and drying, stop using the affected utensils for food.
As for the alternatives:

off.li: Mineral spirits: I would skip them. They dissolve oil, but ordinary hardware-store products are sold as paint solvents and equipment cleaners, without instructions establishing this use on food utensils. Manufacturer’s intended uses.
Vinegar, lemon, salt, or baking soda: They offer no clear advantage for extracting absorbed oil. Dish detergent is the appropriate grease cleaner, and avoids unnecessary abrasion.

off.p: If washing raises a little fuzzy grain, let the wood dry and lightly smooth it with fine sandpaper before oiling.

on.p: I’d start with a gentle hand wash, then switch to food-grade mineral oil once the utensils are completely dry. A single application of olive oil is usually a manageable care mistake.

on.li: Wipe off excess oil with a clean cloth or paper towel.

Wash briefly with warm water and ordinary dishwashing liquid, using a soft sponge or cloth. Rinse thoroughly. Hand washing this way is standard wooden-utensil care; avoid soaking, boiling, and the dishwasher. Wooden utensil maker’s care guidance
Towel-dry immediately, then let them air-dry completely, with air reaching all sides.

If they smell normal and feel clean, apply a light coat of mineral oil specifically labeled food-grade and suitable for cutting boards or utensils. Let it absorb, then wipe off the excess. John Boos care guidance

on.p: Your concern about the pores is valid: washing removes surface oil and some accessible oil; it cannot guarantee removal of everything absorbed into the wood. My recommendation is a practical first step, not a complete extraction procedure. Mineral oil also won’t neutralize any remaining olive oil or prevent it from oxidizing.
On the options you listed:

on.li: Soap and warm water: The best starting point. Detergent helps carry grease away, so vigorous scrubbing is unnecessary. Brief washing followed by prompt drying limits the risk of swelling and cracking.

Mineral spirits: I would avoid them for this job. They are paint-thinning solvents with ingestion and inhalation hazards, and I cannot give you a reliable household procedure for verifying their removal from porous utensils. MedlinePlus

Vinegar, lemon, salt, or baking soda: These are sometimes recommended for stains or odors, but they offer no established advantage for extracting absorbed olive oil. Salt and baking-soda scrubbing add abrasion. John Boos’s stain and odor advice

on.p: If an unpleasant rancid odor persists after washing and thorough drying, hold off on oiling and using them for food. Ask the maker about resurfacing them; sanding may remove affected surface wood, but deeper oil can remain. For a recent light application with no off odor, gentle cleaning and normal care are a reasonable approach.

off.p: Stan and Odete, the likely cause is yeasts or bacteria surviving in the ingredients and then multiplying in the bottled sauce. They consume sugars in the chillies and produce gas. Washing bottles reduces contamination, but it does not preserve the sauce. Small batches may simply be eaten before this becomes noticeable. University of Minnesota’s fermentation guidance

Garlic and chillies in oil also raise a botulism concern if the sauce is insufficiently acidified. Adding lemon juice and vinegar does not, by itself, establish that the whole mixture is acidic enough. Discard the batches that are unexpectedly fermenting; do not taste them to check safety. Botulinum toxin cannot be detected by sight, smell or taste. CDC guidance
For future batches:

off.li: To keep your present recipe: treat it as perishable. Refrigerate immediately at 4°C or below, use within four days, and freeze extra portions. This follows the conservative guidance for homemade garlic-in-oil mixtures. National Center for Home Food Preservation

For bottles stored at room temperature: use a tested preservation recipe and follow its ingredient proportions, container sizes and heat-processing instructions exactly, including altitude adjustments for Johannesburg. A tested Easy Hot Sauce recipe is one option. To bottle your particular oil-containing recipe, have a food-preservation specialist validate its acidity and processing method.
Stop washing the chillies with household bleach. Wash produce under running water. Bottle sanitation cannot replace a safe preservation process. FDA produce guidance

off.p: An equilibrium pH of 4.6 or below is an important botulism control, but measuring that alone does not establish a safe shelf life or prevent all yeast growth; a validated heat process is also needed. University of Minnesota’s canning guidance

on.p: Stan and Odete, your sauce is probably fermenting because yeasts or bacteria survive on the ingredients or enter during preparation, then grow in the bottled sauce. Yeasts can consume the vegetables’ sugars and produce gas. Cleaning the bottles helps, but the sauce itself needs a reliable preservation process. Penn State Extension
Small jars may be eaten before spoilage becomes noticeable. Adding lemon juice and vinegar does not establish that the whole mixture contains enough acid for safe storage.

Garlic and oil need particular care: an inadequately acidified mixture can support bacteria that cause botulism. You cannot judge that risk by smell or taste. For your current recipe, take these precautions:

on.li: Discard batches that have unexpectedly fermented. Do not taste them or try to rescue them by boiling.

Refrigerate fresh sauce immediately at 4°C or colder. Until the recipe has been assessed for safety, use the conservative garlic-in-oil limit of four days, or freeze portions promptly. National Center for Home Food Preservation

For bottles stored at room temperature, use a tested preservation recipe and follow its ingredient quantities, container sizes and heat processing instructions exactly. The NCHFP’s tested hot sauce recipe is one option. Keeping your own formulation requires a food preservation specialist to assess its acidity and processing requirements.
Wash chillies under running water; stop using bleach on them. Household produce washing guidance specifically advises against bleach. FoodSafety.gov

on.p: For keeping your wife’s recipe as it stands, freezing small portions is the most practical option.

off.p: The safest choice is to discard it. Mrs. Richardson’s says to refrigerate its sauces after opening, and I couldn’t find manufacturer guidance confirming that an opened jar is safe after sitting out overnight.
That doesn’t prove it spoiled, but a normal smell or appearance can’t establish safety—so don’t taste it to check. USDA food-safety guidance explains that unsafe food can still look fine.

on.p: The safest choice is to throw it out. Mrs. Richardson’s says its sauces require refrigeration after opening. An overnight stay on the counter exceeds the FDA’s general two-hour limit for foods needing refrigeration.
I can’t confirm that your jar has spoiled, but a normal smell or appearance cannot establish that it’s safe. Don’t taste it to check. (FDA food-storage guidance)

off.p: Use 2 pounds, so about 50 minutes, assuming you’re roasting both pieces side by side in a preheated oven at the recipe’s temperature. Each piece cooks separately; their weights don’t add together for timing.
Leave space between them for heat to circulate. They may take slightly longer together, so treat 50 minutes as an estimate and check each piece with a meat thermometer.
For beef roasts, the USDA recommends 145°F (63°C) in the thickest part, followed by at least a 3-minute rest. USDA temperature guidance

on.p: Use the weight of each piece: 2 pounds, giving an estimated 50 minutes when both cook together in a preheated oven. Leave space between them for heat to circulate. Two separate roasts don’t require doubling the cooking time.

Start checking a little before 50 minutes; thickness and oven performance can affect the timing. Check each piece with a meat thermometer. For beef roasts, USDA recommends 145°F (63°C) in the thickest part, followed by at least 3 minutes of rest. USDA guidance

off.p: Yes—look for a “candy/deep-fry thermometer” with an adjustable pot clip. These are designed to stay in hot oil, leaving your hands free. They’re inexpensive: for example, Taylor’s clip-on model currently lists for US$7.99.

Clip it to the rim with the sensing portion submerged to the manufacturer’s specified depth, clear of the bottom, sides, and chicken. Choose one rated to at least 400°F/200°C, with a stem long enough for your pot.

A digital leave-in probe with a pot clip is another option, especially if you want temperature alarms. Check that it is suitable for frying: a heat-resistant metal probe does not necessarily mean its cable junction can be submerged. ThermoWorks specifically cautions against immersing those junctions in frying oil.
For consistent results, combine the thermometer with a repeatable routine:

off.li: Use the same pot, oil quantity, and batch size. More oil buffers the initial temperature drop, but leave ample room for food displacement and bubbling.
Fry small batches of similarly sized pieces. If the temperature drops substantially and struggles to recover, reduce the next batch.
Follow your recipe’s temperature during cooking. Some chicken recipes preheat to 350°F/177°C, then maintain approximately 325°F/163°C after adding the chicken. Here is one such method.
Adjust the burner in small steps. Expect an initial drop; avoid immediately turning the burner to maximum, since it may overshoot as the oil recovers.
Let the oil return to the starting temperature before each batch.

off.p: Your observation is correct: one fixed burner setting cannot maintain the same temperature under every load. More oil reduces fluctuations; adequate burner power and smaller batches improve recovery. You need a workable temperature range, not a perfectly constant reading.
Finally, use your meat thermometer to check the chicken separately: the thickest part, away from bone, should reach 165°F/74°C. Batter colour alone cannot establish doneness. USDA guidance

on.p: Yes—look for a clip-on candy/deep-fry thermometer. These are designed to stay attached to the pot while the probe sits in hot oil. For an inexpensive example, Taylor’s model 3505 has an adjustable pot clip and a 100–380°F range; its manufacturer currently lists it at US$7.99. Taylor product page

Clip it to the rim with the sensing portion immersed to the depth specified in its instructions. Keep the probe clear of the bottom, sides, and chicken, and keep the dial above the oil. Choose a stem long enough for your pot and oil depth.

A digital leave-in probe with a pot clip is another option. High and low temperature alarms make monitoring easier. Check that the manufacturer explicitly approves the probe for frying oil; the probe’s cable junction may need to stay above the oil even when the metal probe can tolerate the temperature. ThermoWorks frying thermometer guidance
For consistent results:

on.li: Standardize your batches. Use the same pot, oil quantity, and roughly the same weight and size of chicken each time. Keep the chicken refrigerated until preparation.

Preheat to your recipe’s starting temperature. Adding chicken will lower the oil temperature. Some recipes deliberately specify a higher starting temperature than the temperature maintained during frying.

Fry small batches. If the temperature stays too low even with more burner heat, reduce the next batch’s size. More oil helps buffer the initial drop, but your burner still needs to supply enough heat.
Adjust heat gradually and watch the trend. The pot and burner respond with a delay. Ease back as the oil approaches the target, especially when removing a batch.
Let the oil return to the starting temperature before adding the next batch.

on.p: As one concrete example, ThermoWorks’ chicken recipe preheats to 350°F / 177°C, maintains approximately 325°F / 163°C during frying, and reheats to 350°F between batches. Follow the temperatures in your particular recipe. Recipe and temperature guidance

Check chicken separately with your meat thermometer: lift it out and measure the thickest part, avoiding bone. It should reach 165°F / 74°C; crust color alone cannot establish doneness. Leave ample room in the pot for bubbling and oil displacement. USDA frying guidance
For automatic heat adjustment, a thermostatically controlled countertop deep fryer is the next step. It will still experience a temperature drop when food goes in, so batch size remains important.

off.p: Yes—it will probably still turn out! Adding the oil after the flour can mean extra mixing, which may make the cake a little denser or less tender, but it’s unlikely to ruin it. Zucchini adds moisture, too.
If the oil is incorporated and you don’t see oily streaks, stop mixing and bake as usual.

on.p: Yes—it will probably still turn out well! If the oil is mixed in evenly, go ahead and bake it as directed.

Extra beating after adding flour can make the cake a little denser or tougher, but a brief mix to incorporate the oil is unlikely to ruin it. Zucchini adds moisture, too. Stop mixing now that the oil is incorporated.

off.p: Yes—you can use quark, but expect a noticeable texture change, more than a drastic flavor change. Quark is used in baked cheesecakes, though this particular recipe was developed for cream cheese. Nigella’s cheesecake guidance

One important detail: “40%” on quark usually means fat in the dry matter, rather than 40% of the whole product. For example, MILRAM’s 40% quark contains about 10 g fat per 100 g, while Philadelphia block cream cheese contains about 36 g per 100 g. Check your tub’s nutrition panel. MILRAM, Philadelphia
Given that difference, I’d expect:

off.li: Flavor: a little tangier and less buttery. The sugar, vanilla, cream, and browned surface should still give you a familiar cheesecake flavor.
Texture: less silky and rich, with more of a curd-cheesecake texture. Depending on how wet your quark is, it could release some whey; baking it too long could make it grainy or dry.

off.p: If you want to try it with what you have, I’d use 2 lb / approximately 900 g of thick, plain quark. If it has visible whey or is loose, drain it in a cloth-lined sieve in the fridge first, then weigh it. Keep the other ingredients as written for a first attempt—including the heavy cream—and bake until the top is deeply browned but the center still jiggles. Let it cool completely before judging the set.

That’s a reasonable adaptation, not a tested equivalent. It can make a tasty cheesecake, but if the creamy Basque texture is what you especially want, getting cream cheese is the more reliable choice.

on.p: Yes—40% quark should work in this recipe, though you should expect a lighter, less rich cheesecake with a somewhat different texture. The six eggs and ⅓ cup flour give it a good chance of setting successfully. This discussion of the same recipe supports the substitution.

on.li: Taste: Expect a slightly tangier, less buttery filling. With the sugar, vanilla and browned top, I’d expect the difference to be noticeable but pleasant.

Texture: Quark generally contains more moisture than US block cream cheese. The cake may be softer and a little more crumbly or grainy, with less of the smooth, rich mouthfeel of the original. The result will depend on your quark’s consistency. Substitution discussion.

on.p: One relevant label detail: “40%” usually means fat in the dry matter. The actual fat content is much lower; for example, MILRAM’s 40% quark contains 10 g fat per 100 g. Check your tub’s nutrition panel. MILRAM product information.

For your cake, I’d drain the quark overnight in the refrigerator, using a cloth-lined sieve over a bowl, especially if it has visible whey. Then weigh out 2 lb / approximately 907 g of drained quark; you’ll need extra quark to allow for the drained liquid. Keep the remaining ingredients as written for this first attempt.
Bake using the recipe’s visual cues, allowing for a different baking time, and let it cool fully before judging the texture.
